Abstract: Factor models are central to asset pricing and portfolio construction, but neural factors are often difficult to interpret, and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) may address both concerns by describing daily returns across many assets with only a few active features. We ask whether this sparse representation produces stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. We study cryptocurrency returns, use equities as a secondary test, and compare the SAE with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. We find consistently lower volatility in SAE portfolios and link this result to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs. Our contribution is to show that sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, while clearly separating this risk effect from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.
items.author: Weijia Han, Lisha Qu

items.title: Analyzing Condensation on Patterned Surfaces via Deep Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39195v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dropwise condensation is key to power and water systems. State-of-the-art condensation surfaces are often inhomogeneous, either patterned by design or random defects. Inhomogeneous surface features dictate the rates of each stage of dropwise condensation-nucleation, growth, coalescence, and shedding. Characterizing these rates requires the precise detection of thousands of droplets. Yet, existing segmentation methods are unable to detect droplets on inhomogeneous surfaces. We developed TileSAM3, a universal droplet segmentation tool built on the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3). Hierarchical tiling with per-tile inference followed by post-processing extended SAM3's detection cap and raised the effective resolution of small droplets. We created two datasets: High Quality Droplet Dataset (N=365,826; HQDD) with homogeneous surfaces and Low Quality Droplet Dataset (N=63,577; LQDD) with patterned, defect-laden surfaces under adverse lighting. TileSAM3 closely reproduced thresholding annotations on HQDD, surpassed it over sixfold on LQDD (Average Precision 0.57 versus 0.088), and outperformed other deep learning models on all metrics evaluated. Combined with KD-tree tracking, TileSAM3 identified localized nucleation and coalescence in narrow active bands on a stiffness-patterned surface. TileSAM3 enables analysis of understudied inhomogeneous substrates with poor lighting and videography which facilitates faster, lower cost research of condensation materials.
items.author: Tae E. Cooper, Michael Gee, Sheila Whitman, Jemma Dengel, Anthony Katselas, Duygu Dengiz, Frank Keutsch, Joanna Aizenberg

items.title: ACAM-J-MARS: Multi-Atlas Riemannian Spectral Representations for Decoding Advanced Meditation States from fMRI
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inferring jhana-type advanced concentration absorption meditation (ACAM-J) states from fMRI data is challenging due to the spatially distributed nature of meditation-related effects, substantial inter-individual variability that can exceed within-subject state differences, and limited sample sizes. Conventional machine-learning approaches often formulate this problem as unimodal, Euclidean, atlas-based classification, thereby neglecting the non-Euclidean geometry of functional connectivity matrices and underrepresenting temporal information in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI); these limitations can lead to suboptimal classification performance. We propose ACAM-J-MARS (\textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}tlas \textbf{R}iemannian \textbf{S}pectral representation), which computes functional connectivity using multiple atlases, represents symmetric positive definite (SPD) connectivity matrices on a Riemannian manifold, projects them into a log-Euclidean tangent space, and augments connectivity-derived features with low-frequency BOLD spectral energy to better resolve subtle state differences under heterogeneous variability. Evaluated on 204 segments from 22 practitioners, ACAM-J-MARS improves performance across multiple backbone models, achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.757 for early versus late ACAM-J classification and 0.545 for three-class classification, corresponding to a 10.8-point absolute improvement over the strongest baseline. These findings suggest that the proposed representation improves the decoding of advanced meditative brain states and may enable downstream applications such as closed-loop neurofeedback and real-time psychophysiological brain-computer interfaces.
items.author: Jian Wang, Winson F. Z. Yang, Wugeng Zheng, Matthew D. Sacchet

items.title: A Novel Approach to Evaluating Evaluation Metrics for Multi-Output Structured Prediction
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39162v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In multi-output structured prediction tasks, while only one ground truth label may be provided in the training data, multiple equally valid outputs may be possible, making reliable evaluation a persistent challenge. We postulate that human evaluators implicitly use task-specific invariants, e.g., object boundaries in colorized images or named entities in translations, to judge if an output is acceptable. Under this assumption, we introduce a notion of approximate task-specific invariants and use them as diagnostic tools to evaluate a variety of existing metrics for vision and language tasks. We use these task invariants as part of a framework to systematically test metric reliability by encouraging domain-relevant invariants in model outputs via an augmented loss function. In our experiments, we observe that enforcing invariants with an augmented loss yields substantial improvements in popular distributional metrics while more traditional metrics change only marginally. Through this invariants-driven evaluation, we expose where standard metrics fail to detect meaningful differences, and we highlight the conditions under which distributional metrics succeed or still fall short.
items.author: Akshay Vyas, Angelo Pimienta, Nicholas Ruozzi

items.title: Uncertainty-Guided Cross-Modal Alignment for Diffusion-Based IoT Intrusion Detection
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models evolve noisy states toward a learned data distribution, so their sampling behavior depends on the geometry of the representation in which denoising occurs. This dependence is especially important for multimodal data: independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions, while uniform alignment can let an uncertain view distort the shared geometry. To address this gap, we introduce a novel reliability-guided alignment rule that uses normalized VAE posterior variance to control directional cross-modal influence before diffusion training. We study this issue in minority-attack generation for imbalanced Internet-of-Things intrusion detection. Tabular flow attributes, a DeepInsight image, and a packet sequence are encoded by modality-specific variational autoencoders. Per-modality normalized VAE posterior variances provide bounded, sample-specific weighting signals in an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective. We use these quantities as heuristic encoder-derived reliability proxies rather than calibrated probabilistic uncertainties. The full modality-specific latent means obtained after alignment fine-tuning are standardized and modeled jointly by a class-conditional EDM; a second-order sampler then generates paired attack-conditioned latent blocks for the three decoders. In controlled experiments on TON-IoT, uncertainty-aware alignment obtains the highest mean precision, recall, density, and coverage among three diffusion variants. Augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395, and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set. Among the two variants with matched alignment fine-tuning, posterior-variance-based weighting improves both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection relative to uniform weighting.
items.author: Mahdi Arab Loodaricheh, Anita Raja, Mohammad Hossein Manshaei

items.title: Closed Gates Leak: Decomposing Adjacent-Layer Cancellation in Gated Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39068v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In transformer language models with gated multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), adjacent layers write partly against each other into the residual stream. Previous work interpreted this cancellation as layers proposing features and the next layer selectively rejecting the inappropriate ones. We decompose the cancellation by removing the previous layer's write from the input of the next MLP: what the next layer writes along that write splits into what it writes anyway and how much less its MLP writes because the write is present, which we call the damping, and we trace the damping to the neurons that carry it. In gated MLPs the damping is carried by neurons whose gates are closed. SiLU and GELU are slightly negative below zero, so a closed gate still passes a small negative multiple of what the neuron reads, and a neuron whose output weight points along its input weight then subtracts a fraction of the direction it read. Summed over such neurons, closed gates contract the average direction a gated MLP reads, and the previous layer's write is not singled out: the same layer's write at another token is damped as much or more, and the eigenvalue signature from which that work concluded that the correction is selective appears for another token's write as well. Over training the damping grows while what the next layer writes anyway stays flat, and cancellation begins when the damping overtakes it; annealing the negative side of the gate activation away in continued pretraining removes the damping and the cancellation. Adjacent-layer cancellation is therefore weak evidence about which features a model rejects: it is produced by a contraction that gated MLPs apply, on average over directions, to whatever they read.
items.author: Harvey Dam, Ganesh Gopalakrishnan

items.title: BASILISC: Bayesian Alignment of Siamese-Integrated Latents for Inferring Single-cell Correspondence
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-cell assays study the genome one cell at a time. Unimodal assays measure one molecular layer, the newer multimodal assays measure several. Most data are single-modality, so integrating them relies on models trained on multimodal assays, where the cell correspondence across modalities is known. These models return a matching, but rarely a confidence measure. We present BASILISC (Bayesian Alignment of Siamese-Integrated Latents for Inferring Single-cell Correspondence), a framework for matching single-cell representations with uncertainty on the correspondence itself. A BASILISC model is a probabilistic siamese network over the two modalities with a predictive distribution over the correspondence for a cross-modal pair of cells. We instantiate it at two levels: at the cell-type level the question is whether two cells share a cell type, at the cell level which cell is the partner in the other modality. To our knowledge, this is the first uncertainty score on a learned cross-modal correspondence evaluated against a known ground-truth pairing. BASILISC learns a similarity across modalities that reflects cell lineage: an unseen cell type is matched to its lineage relative, matching still works on such held-out types (balanced accuracy 0.86 on unseen against 0.93 on seen types), and the predictive uncertainty rises on these out-of-distribution cells. The uncertainty score also selects high-quality matches for downstream analysis: discarding the least certain fifth of the pairs raises accuracy from 0.93 to 0.98. At the cell level, a deep ensemble of the deterministic matcher reaches 0.062 matching accuracy on the benchmark test set, above the competition winner; on the Bayesian matcher's assignment, the posterior flags the wrong matches that cross a cell-type boundary better than a deterministic read of the same scores (AUROC 0.68 against 0.64).
items.author: Sepideh Saran, Mahsa Ghanbari, Uwe Ohler

items.title: Exponential-Nemytskii Neural Operators: Learning Field Evolution Across Step Sizes
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In variable-step operator learning, agreement at observed step sizes does not by itself determine predictions at other temporal resolutions. We propose an operator whose step-size dependence is prescribed by a first-order Duhamel approximation of semilinear dynamics. It combines exact linear propagation with a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives, allowing evaluation below the observation interval without supervision densely sampled across step sizes. Under suitable conditions and at fixed spatial resolution, we prove that agreement between models at two step sizes controls their prediction differences throughout a prescribed range. We also give conditions for local identifiability of both components from two step sizes, supporting interpretation of the learned structure. A latent extension applies the same construction to learned fields. We evaluate the base model on two synthetic problems and the extension on two real datasets against several baselines.
items.author: Jingye Li, Jinglai Li

items.title: FairSplit: Decomposing the Embedding Space for Fair Classification
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39031v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fair classification faces a twofold challenge: maintaining high classification accuracy while limiting reliance on sensitive information. Our method FairSplit achieves this by learning a decomposition of the embedding space into a Fair Space used for prediction and a Sensitive Space that isolates sensitive information. During training, the model must simultaneously learn the classification task and separate fair from sensitive information. The Sensitive Space gives sensitive attributes a destination, so the Fair Space can be used for prediction without relying on them. This decomposition is guided via a learnable mask and the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) as a measure of statistical dependence. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the demographic parity gap is upper-bounded by both (i) the learned dimensionality of the Fair Space and (ii) the HSIC between the Fair Space and sensitive attributes. FairSplit effectively handles multiclass tasks and non-binary sensitive attributes, overcoming key limitations of existing fair classification methods. Experiments on established fairness benchmarks show that FairSplit achieves competitive accuracy-fairness trade-offs. Code is available at https://github.com/shkabrii/fairsplit.
items.author: Andrii Shkabrii, Anna Beer, Ylli Sadikaj, Claudia Plant

items.title: Fed-IGTD: A federated learning-based framework for tabular-to-image encoding
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tabular-to-image encoding methods, which transform tabular data into image-like representations, have shown promising results in predictive tasks. Despite their benefits, these methods follow a centralized paradigm, in which the data are collected and models are trained on a central device. This raises privacy and security concerns, particularly the risk of data leakage, unauthorized data collection and access to users' private information. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized framework in which multiple clients jointly optimize a shared model without directly sharing training data. We introduce Fed-IGTD, a horizontal FL-based approach in which clients share a common feature space and upload only local statistics, from which the server reconstructs the global correlation matrix and obtains a feature-to-pixel mapping to train a convolutional neural network via Federated Averaging (FedAvg). We studied two differential privacy (DP) mechanisms: (i) a one-shot Gaussian mechanism protecting the correlation-aggregation step; and (ii) a client-level DP-FedAvg variant protecting the training with privacy loss composed via a Renyi-DP accountant. We evaluated Fed-IGTD on five datasets under a systematic sweep of non-IID severity and privacy budgets. Privacy protection applied to the mapping-construction step has little impact on predictive performance. By contrast, DP-FedAvg substantially degrades utility at moderate privacy budgets with a small client cohort (K=5). Ablation study indicates that this degradation is driven mainly by the injected noise rather than by uniform averaging or update clipping. Macro-F1 exhibits sensitivity to performance degradation than accuracy under non-IID heterogeneity and class imbalance.
items.author: David Chushig-Muzo, Eva Milara, Francisco J. Lara Abelenda, Luis Carlos Estrada-Petrocelli, Diego H. Peluffo-Ord\'o\~nez

items.title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling have attracted significant attention as approaches for combining physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning. In this work, we investigate whether these approaches deliver their commonly claimed benefits for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. We develop two hybrid forecasting architectures that integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning. The proposed models are evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries. We assess convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, transferability across geographical regions, and data efficiency. Although the physics-informed models seem to exhibit slightly faster convergence during training, they do not achieve consistent improvements in test-set accuracy, generalization, or performance under limited training data compared to the purely data-driven baseline. These findings suggest that, for modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.
items.author: Peter Pavl\'ik, Franz M. Rohrhofer, Bernhard C. Geiger

items.title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38970v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost.
  Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA.
  We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.
items.author: Martin Isaksson, Rickard C\"oster, \v{S}ar\=unas Girdzijauskas, Seif Haridi

items.title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize.
  We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options.
  Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2\pi X)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.
items.author: Sudipto Guha

items.title: Structural-Test Geometry as an Inductive Bias for Partially Observable World Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories according to distinctions required for later control. With privileged simulator access during training, should response-derived structural information be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry--and how do these choices compare with structured belief distillation? We define posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then train quotient-preserving (QP) world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric. Across a fixed six-task diagnostic suite, the largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points $[21.5,30.7]$ over metric decoding and 6.4 points $[3.8,9.0]$ over structured belief distillation. On GridWorld, metric decoding accurately recovers held-out structural distances ($\rho=.91$) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference $.22$ $[.20,.24]$), showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.
items.author: Todd Y. Zhou

items.title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38901v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/

October 2, 2026
This seminar covers: 
• Why learning-based controllers struggle with real-world deployment: we can’t guarantee a learned policy is safe, and we can’t efficiently find the rare scenarios where it fails
• A new approach that closes the loop between synthesis (building safe policies) and falsification (finding where they break)
• How neural certificates can be formulated as value functions in reinforcement learning, producing control policies with built-in safety and stability guarantees — turning safety into a structural property of the policy rather than a soft penalty
• An adaptive test-case generation method using Bayesian active learning to discover failure scenarios that are both likely to reveal problems and useful for broader coverage
• How this method can predict failures from limited hardware demonstrations
• How it supports scalable, evolving experimental design for system-level testing

items.title: The Biggest Mistake Leaders Make With AI Decisions
items.summary:
What’s the biggest mistake leaders make with AI decisions? Andrew Grotto, co-director of Stanford’s AI, Power, and the New Rules of Global Strategy program, says it’s treating them as technical problems only. Cybersecurity, geopolitics, regulatory policy, and reputational risk all shape those decisions too.

His example is choosing an AI model. Whether a model comes from the U.S., China, or another country, choosing it can also mean taking on that jurisdiction’s regulations, in addition to your own. Organizations that skip that analysis can end up with blind spots in their regulatory risk.

Before Stanford, Grotto served as senior director for cyber policy on the National Security Council at the White House. He leads the program with Francis Fukuyama, senior fellow at Stanford’s Freeman Spogli Institute. Over three and a half days on Stanford’s campus, it helps executives, board directors, and policymakers understand how geopolitical forces are shaping AI decisions.

items.title: Should We Slow Down AI? Francis Fukuyama on the China Question
items.summary:
If the U.S. slows down frontier AI development, will China pull ahead? Francis Fukuyama, senior fellow at Stanford’s Freeman Spogli Institute, says that question comes up every time someone proposes slowing down. He argues that AI is no longer only a technology companies adopt. It has become a major political issue.

He points to recent incidents of AI agents escaping their sandboxes as one reason Washington is paying closer attention. Some AI companies are now asking for more government intervention themselves. For any organization using AI, he says that means understanding the politics of AI at home and, most importantly, internationally.

Fukuyama co-directs Stanford’s AI, Power, and the New Rules of Global Strategy program with Andrew Grotto, former senior director for cyber policy on the National Security Council. Over three and a half days on Stanford’s campus, it helps executives, board directors, and policymakers understand how geopolitical forces are shaping AI decisions.

items.title: Stanford Course Overview: Validation of Safety Critical Systems (AA228V)
items.summary:
Autonomous systems can't be trusted in the real world until you've found how they fail. In this course overview video for Validation of Safety Critical Systems (AA228V), Stanford's Sydney Katz, Lecturer, and Mykel Kochenderfer, Associate Professor, explain how.

Validation of Safety Critical Systems (AA228V) is open now for winter quarter enrollment: https://stanford.io/AA228V

In this course, you'll learn to:
• Use simulation to find failures in autonomous systems before deployment
• Estimate a system's probability of failure with sampling-based methods such as importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo
• Specify safety properties with temporal logic and verify them with formal methods such as reachability analysis

Commercial aviation is one of the safest places you can be, and Kochenderfer credits decades of disciplined verification and validation. In this conversation, he and Katz cover why that playbook isn't enough for the next generation of autonomy: today's AI systems have too many variables to test the old way.

Both Stanford faculty members make the central claim that you have to understand how a system behaves before it goes out into the world. They show how hard it is to specify what you actually want with a wildfire example. A simulated fleet of firefighting drones was rewarded for every grid cell of fire extinguished, so the drones stayed away from the fire, let it burn across the entire map, and then put out as many cells as possible. Keep watching to understand why the objective looked perfectly sensible, but the optimal solution was exactly what no one wanted.

items.title: v2.1.314
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
  • Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
  • Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
  • Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired
  • Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses
  • Fixed claude -p exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1
  • Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and /compact with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting
  • Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family
  • Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's tool_reference blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers
  • Fixed TLS connections failing with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor
  • Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out
  • Fixed claude mcp logout reporting success when the MCP sign-in was not removed, for example while the macOS keychain is locked over SSH
  • Fixed extra sign-in renewals when several sessions share an Anthropic profile login and the credentials lock is busy
  • Fixed claude ultrareview and claude remote-control asking the workspace trust question in a CI job that has a terminal; with CI set they now refuse an untrusted folder at once
  • Fixed an administrator's TLS trust settings in managed settings not being applied in Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed model switching being refused on machines with managed plugin settings when one of your own --plugin-dir or --plugin-url plugins had a broken manifest or failed to download
  • Fixed the Bedrock and Vertex model upgrade offer coming back at every start when managed settings pin the model
  • Fixed forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set only in remote managed settings no longer applying once the stored copy had expired, which let sessions start without policy when the server could not be reached
  • Fixed "Continue automatically at usage limit" continuing more than three times without a prompt from you when a task restarted itself between waits (a /goal check-in, a background or scheduled task)
  • Fixed background and cloud sessions started with Ultracode turning it back on at their next start after it had been switched off
  • Fixed the last broken reply and its retry prompts staying in the conversation after Claude gave up on a tool call that could not be parsed
  • Fixed a PreCompact hook with very large output making compaction fail or repeat; each hook's output is now cut at 10,000 characters
  • Fixed background diff refreshes briefly taking the repository's index lock, which could make a git command run at the same moment fail with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists"
  • Fixed markdown tables jumping between grid and stacked layouts on half-typed rows while streaming, and long tables falling back to raw pipes
  • Fixed the /resume picker showing the text of CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md as a session's title when the session only ran slash commands
  • Fixed /btw answering from the main conversation when asked from a subagent's open transcript
  • Fixed pasting an image over SSH to a Linux machine doing nothing silently; the prompt now says to copy the file over and paste its path
  • Fixed claude remote-control sessions that failed to start when the session service was slow for a moment: the worker's registration is now retried with growing waits
  • Fixed model switches over Remote Control that take over 8 seconds getting a "still pending" error instead of the final result
  • Fixed the sandbox.excludedCommands setting description saying listed commands always run outside the sandbox; it now says every command in a call must match an entry
  • Fixed shell and MCP calls that auto mode, a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook blocked, or that otherwise did not run, reading as if they ran in a collapsed tool group
  • Fixed sandbox protections not applying to a worktree entered by claude -p --resume or --continue
  • Fixed hooks matching Bash not running on shell commands started by the Monitor tool; such hooks can block or ask, but not approve or rewrite those commands
  • Fixed a settings file excluded with --setting-sources still supplying some settings, such as auto mode rules and saved permission consents
  • Fixed auto mode reporting a call as blocked, and listing it in /permissions, when its safety check gave no verdict
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway Vertex upstream hanging for minutes when a Google token endpoint accepts the connection and never answers
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's start-up warning for a deprecated Claude Desktop key that it still serves as written saying "stops being accepted" after the key's end date
  • Fixed /upgrade opening the browser and starting a new login for plans billed through the App Store or Google Play; it now says where to change the plan
  • Fixed --resume, and rewinding past a switch to another model after a refusal, moving a session on a model name Claude Code doesn't recognize to a different model
  • Fixed requests failing when a gateway or cloud provider refuses one of Claude Code's beta headers by name: the request is sent again without it
  • Fixed model IDs spelled with a dot behind an LLM gateway, such as claude-opus-4.8, being treated as an older model with the wrong context window, output limit, effort, thinking mode and cost
  • Fixed Remote Control clients showing a stray "Compacted (ctrl+o to see full summary)" row after /compact
  • Fixed the cloud sessions tip and the Remote Control idle notice showing when an organization's policy turns those features off
  • Fixed a resumed claude.ai cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when the previous worker stopped just after receiving a new chat's files
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions silently dropping a PDF's text past 100,000 characters; it now says how much was unread and where to read on
  • Fixed Claude being told only that a command was declined after you stopped it with Esc or Stop in a cloud session or the IDE; it now also hears that the command may have run
  • Fixed blank lines at the top of a code block disappearing when the code block opens a quote
  • Fixed a blank line appearing above some ⎿ rows in the transcript view (Ctrl+O)
  • Fixed vim mode dw, dW, yw and yW carrying on past the end of the line, and made w and W stop on empty lines
  • Fixed x and Enter in the agent panel sometimes acting on the wrong agent when another agent started or finished
  • Fixed pasted text and dragged-in files being lost in Claude's question dialog unless the "Other" row had focus
  • Fixed pasted text being lost when a row in the prompt footer was selected
  • Fixed vim mode p over a character selection ignoring whether the yanked text was whole lines
  • Fixed vim mode aw and iw taking the line break at the end of a line
  • Fixed ↓ selecting footer items hidden by the ? help menu, the command list or a paste hint
  • Fixed Esc on a command's panel, such as /btw, also interrupting the subagent whose transcript is open
  • Fixed the welcome header in fullscreen mode showing the session's model while viewing a subagent or teammate that runs on a different model
  • Fixed the fullscreen transcript being left mid-conversation after "Restore conversation" in the rewind menu while scrolled up
  • Fixed a rare case where a deleted session could reappear in the resume list as an almost empty entry
  • Fixed prompts containing tags such as <bash-stdout> or <local-command-stdout> not being acknowledged to a local stream-json host
  • Fixed sessions staying untitled when the first prompt failed (for example on a usage limit) and the conversation continued afterward
  • Fixed the skill file watcher checking every removed skill kept in ~/.claude/skills/.trash, which added file system load that grew with each removal
  • Fixed the session name from /rename disappearing while Claude asks for permission or a plan decision, so side-by-side sessions stay identifiable
  • Fixed background sessions that fail to start being reported as a deleted daemon binary when the binary is still on disk
  • Fixed the tip and idle reminder about push notifications appearing when the push settings in /config are hidden or your organization has turned off Remote Control
  • Fixed ~/.claude/skills/.trash and ~/.claude/plugins/.trash growing without limit: each now holds about 1024 entries, whatever cleanupPeriodDays says
  • Fixed the Bash edit diff listing a whole file as changed when a CRLF file under git's line-ending conversion was re-saved unchanged or had one line edited
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an idle session moving to another runner instead of pausing when the runner's request to pause it lost its connection before Anthropic answered
  • Improved memory use in long headless and SDK turns that run many subagents: the parent session no longer keeps each subagent's tool results until the turn ends
  • Improved prompt history: Ctrl+R now matches text inside collapsed [Pasted text] pills
  • Improved the /design-sync upload prompt to show the folder, the project and the files it will upload or delete
  • Improved /permissions review tab, now called Recently blocked: the footer says what Esc will do with marked rows
  • Improved auto mode's blocked calls: messages name the command, say Claude may retry and auto mode checks again, and point to /permissions to review
  • Improved permission prompts: a long reason takes fewer rows, so it pushes the command being approved off the screen on fewer terminals
  • Improved the cloud session error shown while a request refused for your claude.ai login is still being retried: it now also suggests claude auth login
  • Improved the behavior of stored claude.ai, Team, and Enterprise logins when MDM and remote settings differ on base URL or apiKeyHelper
  • Improved /config in agent view to say how to stop agent view opening by default
  • Improved session auto-titles: a session that starts with a skill or a prompt-based command such as /security-review now gets a title from it instead of staying untitled
  • Improved --resume speed and memory use on damaged transcripts
  • Improved /context speed in sessions with ten thousand or more MCP tools
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved the error shown when a session's branch isn't on the git remote: it now covers a never-pushed branch, says how to fix each case, and no longer suggests retrying
  • Updated the /claude-api skill: its Datadog setup for API tracing now sends the dd-llmobs-enabled: true header, as the Console does, and its ant install instructions drop the outdated macOS xattr step
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to advise printing y-axis tick labels in full under 10,000, and horizontal ones in full under a million where they fit
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to answer donut and pie chart requests with ranked bars or a segmented bar that prints its values
  • Changed Claude's file tools to ask before editing the local copy of your organization's server-managed settings, as they do for your settings files
  • Changed /ultrareview to check workspace trust before it runs git, as claude ultrareview does
  • Changed the Bash tool's shell to clear any inherited which alias or function and to stop passing exported which/unsetenv functions to commands, so which is the system command or zsh builtin
  • Changed /permissions Recently blocked to refuse approving a call you can't read in full, including one the terminal is too short to show
  • Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a hook's allow of an MCP tool call now counts as no answer, so the classifier or a permission prompt decides
  • Changed hook if conditions such as Monitor(tail *) to match the Monitor tool's shell commands as Bash(tail *) matches Bash's
  • Changed the claude-api skill to ask to read a Managed Agents workflow run's workflow before changing the agent to improve that run
  • Changed flagged requests to retry on another model, not end in a refusal, when ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, availableModels or deniedModels leaves only an older Opus model, or none
  • Changed idle compaction to also run for subscribers with telemetry turned off, and on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and LLM gateways once the one-hour prompt cache is on
  • Changed FORCE_HYPERLINK=false (also no and off) to turn hyperlinks off instead of on
  • macOS: Changed git grep in most commands that Claude runs to use the C locale, to avoid a reported memory leak in macOS's regex library on files that aren't valid UTF-8
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Clear authentication" for MCP servers reporting success when the saved sign-in could not be removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed missing spinner and Stop button while a queued message's hooks run
  • [VSCode] Fixed session group changes that cannot be saved, such as a delete, failing silently; an error notification now appears
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+F / Ctrl+F not opening the find widget in the plan preview tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed the voice dictation shortcut (Ctrl+D) doing nothing under non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew
  • [VSCode] Fixed missed one-time saved scheduled tasks being deleted without asking when the extension opened without a chat
  • [VSCode] Changed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CFC_PROMPT to also stop the extension adding the Claude in Chrome instructions to a session's messages; the browser tools stay available
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an Include completed button to the Scheduled tasks page when finished one-off tasks are the only ones hidden, so you can show them without opening the Sort menu
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed recently used self-hosted environments never appearing among the recent environments on the new session card
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud sessions reporting uncommitted changes every turn after Claude moved a branch to a commit it had pushed from another worktree
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings squeezing its content out of view in very short windows or at high zoom; the dialog now scrolls
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the permission mode picker staying on Auto after a running cloud or Remote Control session refused the switch; it now shows the mode in use and tells you
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved scheduled tasks: runs in Anthropic's cloud now load the plugins enabled on your claude.ai account
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved Test connection for GitHub Enterprise in admin settings to also connect the way cloud sessions do, and to warn you when that second test fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved cloud session transcripts: a rename row now names the new title, and repository and environment lists show as a table instead of one line of JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed cloud sessions from the web, desktop and mobile apps to start even when a setup script exits with an error, instead of failing to start
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the permission mode button in Remote Control sessions showing the wrong mode until you typed; while your computer is online it now shows the real mode on open
  • [Claude Tag] Added a dismissible link to the Claude Tag API docs on the Bundles and Channels tabs in admin settings, for Enterprise organizations with Slack connected
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed @Claude !restart giving up after one failed workspace check in channels shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces; it now retries, then asks you to run it again
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a second confirmation DM and channel note when you connect your Claude account from Slack twice from the same link within a few minutes
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed follow-up messages in Slack showing no sign of progress while Claude's session waits for a self-hosted runner; Claude now posts a wait notice in the thread
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude sometimes not answering a tag in its own thread in Slack Connect channels where both organizations have installed Claude
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Retry on plugin and skill pages in Claude Tag admin settings discarding unsaved access changes after a failed load; your edits now stay in place
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the repositories control in Claude Tag admin settings showing the same action twice; its menu now lists only what the button doesn't already do

items.title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97
items.summary:
Host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting.

The post Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97 appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
What’s new in research? 

You may already be familiar with the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab) on LinkedIn. Now, you can catch up on highlights from across the research community at Microsoft on our social channels, YouTube, and major podcast platforms, too. 

In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus, host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting. 

Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next.

Related links:

  • Research Focus newsletter on LinkedIn (opens in new tab)
  • ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents
  • Code Understanding is a Bottleneck for Coding Agents
  • TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills from Offline Telemetry
  • Why Copilot use looks so similar across industries, and what that misses (opens in new tab)
  • Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
  • New AI framework bridges a critical gap in mid-range weather forecasts
  • BioEmu2 in public preview (opens in new tab)

Chapters

00:48: A self-improving agentic framework (opens in new tab)

01:35: Understanding coding agent success and failure  (opens in new tab)

02:29: Evolving agent skills with activity logs  (opens in new tab)

03:22: Looking beyond similarities in AI use  (opens in new tab)

04:15: Helping teachers make more time for teaching  (opens in new tab)

04:52: Improving extended-range weather forecasting  (opens in new tab)

05:42: BioEmu2 now available in public preview  (opens in new tab)

06:32: Final thoughts (opens in new tab)

Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:

  • Apple Podcasts
  • Email
  • Android
  • Spotify
  • RSS Feed

Transcript

[MUSIC]

SOWBHAGYA SURESH: Hi, I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Welcome to Microsoft Research Focus.

You’ve probably read our newsletter. And now you can get highlights from across the research community at Microsoft here, on YouTube, and major podcast platforms. Whether you read, watch, or listen to it, Research Focus is your source for research news at Microsoft.

Coming up in this edition: what everyday AI use reveals about the way we work; how a new AI model could help scientists better understand proteins; a new approach to improving weather forecasts weeks in advance; and more. So here’s what’s new.

A self-improving agentic framework

More and more, AI agents are handling tasks that are complex.

[MUSIC FADES]

Tasks that require multiple steps, decisions, and interactions with external tools. But how can we count on AI agents to do the work if their ability to adjust when things go wrong may require a lot of resources with no guarantees of a better result?

A new self-improving framework called ForkPilot learns when it’s worth revisiting earlier decisions to find a different approach and adapts its strategy based on new outcomes.

Tested across six benchmarks and leading AI models, ForkPilot measures up to the best existing methods while reducing AI processing demands by up to 59%. These results suggest that AI agents can solve complex problems more reliably and efficiently, making them more practical and cost-effective to deploy at scale.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Understanding coding agent success and failure

Coding agents execute user queries by reasoning about, editing, and running code. Understanding why these agents fail is critical if we want to build more capable and reliable coding agents. Unfortunately, existing benchmarks often make it difficult to identify which factors contribute to success or failure.

CABRA is a framework for generating coding challenges from scratch. It lets researchers increase complexity in a controlled way and pinpoints the skills that are most difficult for agents.

Across thousands of generated challenges, the researchers found that agents often overcame coding problems by using tools. Yet the agents still struggled when they needed to understand unfamiliar codebases. The findings suggest that understanding existing code, rather than modifying it, remains one of the biggest obstacles to developing more effective coding agents.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Evolving agent skills with activity logs

Computer-use agents are AI systems that are designed to complete tasks that require clicking and typing. They can fill in forms, process requests, and navigate websites. To do this effectively, they need to learn the procedures that people use to get work done. User activity logs can offer a way to capture this knowledge. But activity logs typically don’t record the intent behind each action and often combine tasks.

The new framework TeleTune learns reusable skills and workflows from these logs. It also infers the task goals associated with the sequences of actions.

In evaluations across software and browser tasks, TeleTune outperformed existing approaches. By learning from existing activity, TeleTune offers a scalable way to help AI agents adapt to unfamiliar software and carry out complex, multi-step workflows

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Looking beyond similarities in AI use (opens in new tab)

Workers across industries may appear to be using AI in surprisingly similar ways, but a closer look reveals a different story.

Microsoft researchers analyzed aggregated Copilot Chat activity across a broad range of customer categories and found that editing documents led all classified activities, accounting for more than 20 percent.

But when researchers set aside the 20 most common activities, differences between customer categories became substantially more pronounced. The most common uses of AI may be hiding important differences in how organizations use it for more specialized work.

For business leaders, the takeaway is clear: don’t assume you have the same AI needs as others in your industry. Finding the right opportunities means looking beyond usage statistics to understand what employees actually do, how they work, and what outcomes matter most.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Helping teachers make more time for teaching

A new study shows how Shiksha Copilot—a human-in-the-loop AI tool—could transform teacher workflows in Global South classrooms.

The study in low-resource schools in India found the tool reduced the time teachers spent on bilingual lesson planning and bureaucracy. That gave them more time to craft more engaging classroom activities.

More than a thousand teachers participated, and many reported reduced stress levels and a positive impression of how AI can help them. These teachers actively engaged with Shiksha Copilot, using their professional expertise to adapt and repurpose materials to suit their own classrooms.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

Improving extended-range weather forecasting 

Ten-day weather forecasts have become remarkably dependable. But what about the weeks that follow?

The two-to-six-week window remains a major challenge for forecasting models, which is a problem. That’s when a wide range of critical decisions get made related to farming, managing wildfires, and preparing for extreme weather.

A new machine-learning framework called Probabilistic Bias Correction, or PBC, is helping close that gap. PBC learns from a weather model’s past mistakes and helps correct them.

And the early results are promising.

PBC took top honors in a global competition focused on improving extended-range forecasting. It’s also being deployed in Kenya, where it’s helping improve critical monsoon forecasts for farmers.

This development could help make weather predictions more useful across a broad range of applications.

[TRANSITION MUSIC]

BioEmu2 now available in public preview (opens in new tab)

BioEmu2, a new foundation model for understanding biomolecular structure, dynamics, and function, is now available in public preview.

Developed by the Microsoft Research AI for Science team, BioEmu2 builds on Biomolecular Emulator, a deep-learning model designed to help scientists better understand how proteins work.

That understanding could have important implications for medicine. By learning more about how proteins function, scientists could move closer to developing more effective medications that enhance beneficial protein activity or prevent proteins from causing harm.

Go to the BioEmu2 Microsoft Research GitHub repository (opens in new tab) to explore the model and learn more.

[MUSIC]

And that’s your Research Focus.

From more capable AI agents to better weather forecasting, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring at Microsoft.

Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by following Microsoft Research on major social platforms.

I’m Sowbhagya Suresh. Thanks so much for tuning in. We’ll see you in the next Microsoft Research Focus.

[MUSIC FADES]
Opens in a new tab

The post Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #97 appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.title: Managed Deep Agents v0.10: Browser use and asynchronous subagents
items.summary:
• Browser use: Your agent can book travel or file a claim on sites that have no API. When a site asks you to sign in, the agent hands you the browser window, so your password stays out of the model's messages and traces.
  • Async subagents: A long job can go to a subagent that runs in the background while your agent keeps talking with you. You can ask the agent to check on the job or change its course, and the result comes back to the conversation when the subagent finishes.
  • Thread origins and stopping runs: Replies go back to the Slack thread a request started in, including replies from a scheduled run or from a subagent that finished later. A Stop button in the thread cancels its runs.

‍

Managed Deep Agents v0.10 is out today. It adds browser use, so your agent can work on websites that have no API, and async subagents, which run long tasks in the background while your agent keeps talking to you.

In this post, we cover why agents need each one and how to turn it on, then the rest of the release.

Give your agent a browser

Booking travel, canceling a subscription, or filing a claim all happen on sites built for people clicking through pages, and there's often no API an agent can call. While agents can reason through how to complete the task, they can’t take action on websites without an API. Fetching the page with curl doesn't get far either, it produces HTML before any JavaScript renders the page and the agent can't click anything.

Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse can browse websites to unlock a broader set of use cases, and DataDomesaw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Coding agents need a browser too, to check that a change to an app actually renders and works.

We cover where a browser helps and how it works under the hood in “Browser use in Managed Deep Agents”. To turn it on, declare a browser at your project root:

# browser.py
from managed_deepagents import define_browser

browser = define_browser(scope="thread", idle_ttl_seconds=600)

Managed Deep Agents runs the browser in its own LangSmith sandbox and adds the following browser tools to your agent automatically:

ToolWhat it doesbrowser_snapshotReads the page's accessibility tree and assigns element IDsbrowser_runNavigates and interacts, through JavaScript or batches of actions against snapshot IDsbrowser_screenshotCaptures the page, optionally saving the image to the sandboxbrowser_handoffGives a person control of the window

By default, each conversation gets its own browser, which is reused across turns and starts with no cookies or logins from other threads. With scope="user", each signed-in person gets one browser whose logins carry across all of their conversations, so the agent only asks them to sign in to a site once.

Hand the browser to a person

Most browser agents stop at a login wall or a two-factor prompt. With browser_handoff, the agent hands the window to you instead, so your password never ends up in the model's messages or traces.

The agent calls browser_handoff(reason) and explains why it needs you. Your agent channels — like Slack and Studio — will show have a link to allow users of your agents to hand off browser control natively, which opens a link to interact with the remote browser and a Hand back button . Custom clients can render the handoff artifact themselves. Once you sign in and hand control back, the agent checks the page to see whether the login worked and continues. Handoff returns immediately, so the agent can do other work while it waits. Handoff links expire after 15 minutes.

Handoffs let your agent use a webpage for you, without seeing your credentials.

The browser use docs cover scopes, per-run configuration, and the full handoff flow.

Run subagents in the background

Subagents let an agent hand a focused task to a helper with its own context window. Previously in Managed Deep Agents, subagents ran inline, so the agent called one and waited for its answer. This works for a quick lookup, and still is a supported pattern. But for a long task backed by a synchronous agent, or where multiple agents need to be fanned out, the person talking to the agent waits too, and additional interactions with the orchestrator agent are blocked.

With Managed Deep Agents v0.10, you can run subagents asynchronously, without blocking the orchestrator agent, by adding async to a subagent definition:

from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent

agent = define_deep_agent(
    name="research-assistant",
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    subagents=[
        {
            "name": "researcher",
            "description": "Researches a topic in the background.",
            "system_prompt": "Research the topic and report your findings.",
            "async": True,
        },
    ],
)

The agent starts an async subagent on its own thread and can keep talking to the user while the subagent(s) run(s). The orchestrator agent starts, checks on, updates, and cancels these tasks with a set of async task tools. Every served agent also gets a background copy of a general-purpose subagent, so it can choose at runtime whether to run delegated work in the foreground or the background.

Async subagents notify the agent on their own, so the agent never sits in a polling loop. What happens next depends on what the agent is doing when a subagent finishes:

When the subagent finishes, the agent isWhat happensBusyIt checks unfinished tasks before each model call, so the result arrives mid-runIdleThe subagent wakes it with a new runPaused on an approvalThe approval is left alone; the result arrives once the user answers

An async subagent shares the agent's sandbox, so it picks up the files the agent already wrote. Its run appears under the agent's run in LangSmith. In Slack, its approvals post back to the original thread, and answering them there resumes the subagent.

Also in v0.10

  • runtime.thread: every thread now carries a record of where it started, such as a Slack thread, and who is on it. Tools can read runtime.thread on any run, which is how a Studio resume, a scheduled run, and an async subagent's wake-up run all reply in the original Slack thread.The runtime docs cover the managed fields tools can read.
  • Stopping runs: Slack threads get a native Stop button that cancels the thread's runs, and Studio can cancel runs on Slack threads.
  • Slack channel handlers (experimental): onEvent decides what each Slack event starts, including mentions, direct messages, other messages, and button clicks. status sets what Slack shows while a run works, and reply: "none"leaves replying to the agent. See the Slack channel docs.
  • Bring your own Slack app: mda deploy asks which app a new Slack channel should use. You can pick one that LangSmith creates and manages, create a new one from a manifest, or use one you already have.
  • resolveUser: when someone messages your agent in a channel like Slack, Managed Deep Agents verifies who sent it. resolveUser maps that sender to the matching user in your own system, so your tools can look up that person's account and permissions. Write it as a function or point it at an endpoint we call, and set it on the identitydeclaration to cover every channel or on a single channel.
  • Breaking changes: connectors.mcp() and the connectors/ layout have been removed. MCP servers must be declared in tools/mcp.ts or tools/mcp.py. The sandbox scope option is also removed. For LANGSMITH_*variables, shell environment variables now win over a project .env.

Getting started

Managed Deep Agents v0.10 is available in public beta today. Start from the docs, or create a new project:

uvx --from managed-deepagents mda init my-agent
cd my-agent
uv run mda deploy

As always, we can't wait for you to tell us what you build.

ICYMI: v0.9 added agent-created schedules, per-run configuration, and Slack reactions. Read the v0.9 post.

‍
