items.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
items.summary:
Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details [...]

Read More...

The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests).
  • Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production.
  • Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests.

Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale.

Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch.

In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives.

The Advantage of Catching JiTTests

Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not.

How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta

JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives).

It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers?

To address this, we developed two tandem workflows:

  • An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points.
  • A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”).

To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives.

We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch.

How It Works

The entire system workflow happens in five stages:

Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering 

The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions.

Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows

The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them.

At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent.

Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent).

Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches.

Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment)

Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive).

The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review:

  • The weak-catch test-case code.
  • The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace).
  • The code changes between parent and child (the diff).
  • The inferred diff intent.

Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake)

We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake).

LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration.

Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out)

Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers.

Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output.

The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta

With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results.

As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives.

In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe.

Why It Matters

Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. 

Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended.

The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item.

Read the Paper

Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure.

The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Browser Use in Managed Deep Agents
items.summary:
• A browser lets agents do work on the web that APIs can't cover, including clicking, scrolling, and filling out forms.
  • Managed Deep Agents now runs a browser for your agent, with tools tuned for context-efficient browser use.
  • Managed Deep Agents ships with support for thread and user scoped browser sessions. Handoffs allow users to log into and interact with websites with credentials persisted across sessions.

Agents have gotten good enough to work where we work, and a lot of that work happens in a browser. Booking travel, canceling a subscription, or filing a claim all happen on sites built for people clicking through pages, including ones the agent didn't plan to visit. Often there's no API an agent can call. Fetching the page with curl doesn't get far either, since it returns the HTML before any JavaScript renders the page and can't click anything.

Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse already work this way. Browser agent traffic is growing fast too, and DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone.

Managed Deep Agents lets you build and deploy agents in LangSmith without running any infrastructure. You write the agent's instructions and tools, and LangSmith runs the harness and runtime. Today, we're giving these agents a browser, so you can build your own agents that work on the web. Managed Deep Agents runs the browser too, and gives your agent tools tuned for it.

In this post, we cover where a browser helps and how to turn it on, including handing the browser to a person when the agent needs one. Then we walk through how it works under the hood. Agents built with open source Deep Agents can use a browser too. We'll cover how we tested and tuned the browser tools in a deep dive next week.

Where a browser helps

With a browser and tools to drive it, an agent can read what renders on a page and click through it, the same way you (a human) would.

So far, two common use cases have emerged:

  • Actions an API can't cover, like booking a flight or a restaurant reservation. When a site does have an API for the task, the agent should use the API.
  • End-to-end testing, like checking a frontend change before it merges. When a pull request changes a signup form, a coding agent can start the app in its sandbox, open the form in a browser, and click through it to check that the change works. We use this in Open SWE, our coding agent.

Adding browser use capabilities

To add a browser, export a browser from browser.py at the project root:

# browser.py
from managed_deepagents import define_browser

browser = define_browser(
    scope="thread",
    idle_ttl_seconds=600,
)

scope controls how browser sessions are shared.

  • scope="thread" (the default) gives each thread its own browser. Every conversation starts with a fresh browser window, with no cookies or logins left over from another thread.
  • scope="user" shares one browser across a signed-in user's threads (see Identity). Each thread gets its own window, so two conversations running at once don't click over each other, but they share cookies and other browser state. If you sign in to a site in one thread, a later thread can pick up that session instead of starting over.

The browser stops after idle_ttl_seconds without activity (10 minutes by default), so you don't pay for a browser nobody is using.

Hand off the browser to a user

Some steps still need a person, and signing in is the most common one. You don't want to give the agent your password, where it would end up in the model's messages, in traces, and with a model provider.

So when the agent hits a login page, it calls browser_handoff with a reason, like "Please sign in to Acme Travel so I can continue." In LangSmith Studio, the UI where you chat with and debug your agent, you get an interactive card with the same browser. You sign in yourself, click Hand back, and the agent picks up where it left off, already signed in. Handoff comes with every managed browser and works automatically in Managed Deep Agents channels like Slack, so there's nothing extra to set up.

This matters most with scope="user". With user scope, the sign-in carries over to your later threads, so the agent asks you to log in once, the same way your own browser remembers you.

How it works under the hood

An agent needs two things to use the web: a browser, and a toolset to drive it. Managed Deep Agents manages both.

The browser. Managed Deep Agents runs the browser in its own LangSmith sandbox, separate from the agent. It's a remote browser, so nothing runs on your machine. Unlike most remote browsers, it also has a private link to the agent's sandbox, which is what makes end-to-end testing work (more below).

The tools. Managed Deep Agents adds the browser tools to the agent:

  • browser_snapshot reads the page's accessibility tree and labels interactive elements with IDs.
  • browser_run acts on the page, either with a batch of actions like click and fill or with JavaScript that uses a Playwright-style page object, which Stagehand translates into its own commands.
  • browser_screenshot captures the rendered page.
  • browser_handoff passes the browser to a person, who hands it back when they're done (see above).

browser_run does most of the work. It takes code, so the agent can write a whole chain of steps (open a page, fill a field, click, check the result) as one call and return only what it needs. That keeps long browser tasks fast, and it keeps most of the page out of the agent's context.

The tools are built on Stagehand, Browserbase's open source SDK for building browser agents. We tested and tuned them with the agent development lifecycle: running browser benchmarks, reading the traces in LangSmith, and validating each change with evals. On 100 tasks from WebVoyager, a benchmark of everyday tasks on live websites, they passed 90% of tasks for $1.98 in total. That was the highest pass rate of the seven toolsets we tested. The closest, Browserbase's MCP server, passed 89% at 9x the cost.

This setup supports both use cases, in slightly different ways.

Actions an API can't cover

For tasks like booking a reservation, the agent only needs the browser. Its browser tools send commands to the browser sandbox, which drives the page.

End-to-end testing

End-to-end testing needs one more piece. The app under test runs in the agent's own sandbox, so the browser has to reach it. Two connections make that work:

  • The agent controls the browser through its browser tools, as above.
  • The browser reaches the app through a localhost bridge. When the browser opens localhost:5173, the request travels over a private link to port 5173 in the agent sandbox. The app doesn't need a public URL. Here, localhost means the agent's sandbox.

The agent starts the app with execute, opens it in the browser, clicks through real flows like a signup form, and checks what renders.

Once a test passes, you can ask the agent to save its steps as a test file, since each browser_run call is a piece of an ordinary Playwright script. Later runs replay that file with no model calls until the page changes.

Conclusion

Browsers open up a huge part of the web to agents, from booking a flight to testing the app a coding agent just built. With Managed Deep Agents, giving your agent a browser takes a few lines of code, and the tools behind it are tuned to be fast and context-efficient.

Add a browser to a managed agent with define_browser. To give an open source deep agent a browser, where you bring your own (like a hosted one from Browserbase), see the browser use guide.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Sean McGuire, Miguel Gonzalez, and Kyle Jeong from Browserbase for their help with Stagehand and this post.

Slice Into GFN Thursday: ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches on GeForce NOW
items.summary: This Halloween week, GFN Thursday is delivering a fresh batch of gaming treats. Something wicked this blade comes. items.content:
This Halloween week, GFN Thursday is delivering a fresh batch of gaming treats.

Something wicked this blade comes. S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches on GeForce NOW today, bringing a scarily good blend of martial arts and punk fantasy to the cloud.

There’s also something on the horizon for adventurers: World of Warcraft: Forever arrives Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 3 p.m. PST, with a launch-week access reward coming for GeForce NOW members.

This week’s lineup also includes nine games streaming from the GeForce NOW library, alongside new mod support for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. That means more options to play, with no downloads or installs to haunt gamers’ devices.

There’s another sweet update for gamers in India: The option to sign up for four-month Performance and Ultimate memberships is launching tomorrow. Visit the GeForce NOW website for more information.

Cold Steel Meets Cloud Power

Framed for his master’s murder and gravely wounded, a warrior named Soul has 66 days to uncover a conspiracy threatening the martial world in S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero. Powered by Unreal Engine 5, the game combines wuxia storytelling with cinematic action.

Master more than 30 primary weapons and over 20 Phantom Edges, chaining evasions, deflections and counterattacks into fluid combat. Traditional Chinese martial arts meet mechanical prosthetics, industrial ruins and rock music in a distinctive kungfupunk world.

Ultimate members can wield GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, compatible TVs and more. GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage, leaving more time for the next clash. Soul’s clock is ticking, but the download bar doesn’t have to. Cut to the chase and hop into the game today.

Azeroth Awaits

Get ready for Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever, arriving Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 3 p.m. PT, on GeForce NOW. Explore an iconic world reimagined with new and expanded zones, new gameplay enhancements, upgraded graphics and more.

A new reward will give eligible GeForce NOW members access to join beginning at launch and ending Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT. The reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers for new WoW users who don’t already have a subscription, while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis.

Once available, members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem. Mark the calendar and gather the party — launch week is approaching.

New Tricks and Treats

Familiar favorites have a few new tricks, too: Mod.io support is now available directly in game for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered, bringing more ways to make Night City and the Continent feel different.

And the treats keep coming with the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:

  • Phantom Blade Zero (New release on Steam, Oct. 28)
  • ATMOSFAR (New release on Steam, Oct. 29)
  • Hunting Simulator 3 (New release on Steam, Oct. 29)
  • Queen’s Domain (New release on Steam, Oct. 30)
  • Dimraeth (Steam)
  • Dressmaker (Steam)
  • Halloween (Epic Games Store)
  • Hell Let Loose: Vietnam (Epic Games Store)
  • The Seance of Blake Manor (Steam)

Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles.

Settle in for a scary-good gaming session: Grab a day pass to experience Performance or Ultimate cloud gaming. Gamers can then apply the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership upgrade.

What’s haunting the gaming playlist this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

Building Evidence-Grounded Agent Memory with OpenWiki and Graphs
items.summary:
• A compiled wiki gives agents domain context that retrieval alone must reconstruct. On questions spanning multiple sources, an agent using OpenWiki as a memory layer was 5x more accurate than one using grep tools alone.
  • Adding an evidence graph helps agents follow the wiki back to supporting evidence. We turned citations and document references into explicit graph edges agents could follow. Compared with the wiki alone, this doubled how consistently the agent cited the same evidence, improved accuracy by 27%, and cut cost per correct answer by 58%.
  • Save compiled memory for repeated cross-source reasoning. The wiki captures domain knowledge and complex relationships. Adding an evidence graph improves accuracy and retrieval consistency. For simple lookups, however, the agent without memory was just as accurate and faster.

Agents working across an organization’s policies, manuals, wikis, tickets, and code must navigate knowledge scattered across systems and teams. Finding a relevant passage is only the start. They also need to determine which rules apply, what has changed, and how one source affects another.

A persistent memory layer preserves knowledge and relationships for agents to reuse across tasks. Without it, agents often have to reconstruct that understanding on every question, making their work expensive and error-prone. This is especially challenging in banking and insurance, where policies and guidelines frequently amend or supersede one another.

We tested OpenWiki, our open-source wiki compiler, as this memory layer. On questions requiring connections across sources, the wiki made the agent roughly 5x more accurate than search alone. Adding an evidence graph that connects wiki statements to supporting passages and links related sources improved accuracy a further 27% and doubled citation consistency.

Why a compiled wiki?

RAG pipelines often use semantic or hybrid search to retrieve isolated chunks, leaving agents to piece together how those chunks relate. We’ve explored improving retrieval with agentic RAG and graph-based metadata filtering, but finding relevant passages is only part of the work. Cross-source questions require tracing references, resolving conflicting rules, and understanding dependencies. Memory preserves that understanding so agents don’t have to rebuild it on every question.

A compiled wiki provides that memory layer by synthesizing source material into linked pages that explain key concepts and their relationships. The wiki is updated as sources change, giving agents context they can reuse.

OpenWiki, our open-source CLI built on Deep Agents, creates these wikis with citations back to the sources. We originally built it so coding agents wouldn’t have to rediscover architecture and code behavior on every task.

Every OpenWiki statement rests on a claim, an assertion linked to supporting source lines and their hash. When those lines change, the hash changes, allowing OpenWiki to flag affected claims without a model call, saving on token costs and making staleness detection more deterministic. Only those claims go to a model for confirmation, revision, or retraction, allowing the memory layer to self-correct as its sources change. We explain this in Building self-correcting memory in OpenWiki.

Building the test document library

We built a synthetic insurance document library of 111 long-form documents. We chose insurance because policies and endorsements frequently reference, amend, and override one another; this is exactly the kind of cross-document dependency that makes retrieval hard.

To score the benchmark, we created a ledger of 972 facts and controlled where each fact should appear, how documents referenced each other, and what changed between versions. We generated the surrounding prose with an LLM and ran automated checks to ensure the required facts were present.

Finally, we made the corpus intentionally messy, mixing in outdated versions, contradictions, indirect reference chains, varied wording, and very long documents to better match what agents face in real enterprise libraries.

How we configured our experiment

We evaluated the same retrieval agent under two conditions: Search (keyword search over the original documents) and Wiki (the same agent with access to an OpenWiki-compiled, source-linked wiki). The underlying model, instructions, documents, and questions were held constant — only the agent’s access to compiled memory changed.

We tested 80 simple lookup questions and 50 connected questions that require following dependencies across documents (e.g., identifying what depends on a provision or is affected when it changes). We asked each question three times to measure run-to-run variation.

Metrics (what “better” means):

  • Accuracy (0–1): a grader checked answers and quoted evidence against a checklist from the 972-fact ledger (rewarding required facts and penalizing contradictions).
  • Consistency (0–1): overlap of cited evidence across the three runs (average pairwise Jaccard similarity of citation sets). This measures whether the agent reliably grounds its answers in the same sources, not whether the answers are correct.
  • Cost + latency: model spend (USD) and wall-clock time per question.

Where the wiki helped, and where it struggled

OpenWiki compiled the 111-document library into a wiki roughly one-tenth its original size for $4.15. Adding 17 documents later cost about $0.09 each. The analysis below excludes compilation and update costs, reporting only retrieval and answering costs.

We used simple lookups as a control. These single-passage questions require little cross-document insurance context, so we didn’t expect the wiki to help much. Results were similar for search and wiki, respectively (0.84 vs 0.83 accuracy; 0.72 vs 0.74 citation overlap; $0.020 vs $0.021 per correct answer), while latency increased from 9 to 12 seconds.

Connected questions required reasoning across sources using domain-specific relationships. Here, the wiki improved accuracy roughly 5x, from 0.10 with search alone to 0.52. Its compiled context helped the agent apply domain knowledge and find relevant relationships with fewer tool calls, cutting cost per correct answer from about $0.55 to $0.19.

Despite these accuracy and cost gains, the wiki agent’s evidence retrieval remained inconsistent. Citation overlap dropped from 0.74 on simple lookups to 0.25 on connected questions. Citation stability doesn’t measure correctness, but changing evidence can change an answer, especially when sources conflict. For critical business functions, teams need answers they can reproduce and audit, not just better average accuracy.

The wiki helped the agent apply domain knowledge across sources. The remaining challenge was making the path to supporting evidence more repeatable.

Adding an evidence graph

To make retrieval more consistent, we added a lightweight evidence graph: a map that turns wiki citations into explicit, typed edges between claims, wiki pages, paragraphs, and topics. OpenWiki citations are text references in Markdown files. The graph makes them durable by materializing them as typed edges. That gives the agent a stable path to follow instead of rediscovering the same links with search.

We built this graph in two steps:

  1. Store every paragraph as a new primitive. A deterministic process splits each document into paragraphs and assigns each a unique identifier. These paragraphs become atomic units of information, linking claims to exact supporting passages rather than entire documents.
  2. Connect the passages with typed edges. We linked paragraphs, claims, and wiki pages with typed edges: claims cite paragraphs, newer documents supersede older ones, and sections refers_to other documents. Each edge identifies the relationship, not just the connection. We built edges two ways. Some are extracted deterministically from document references. Because wiki claims already carry text citations, we can materialize typed edges like refers_to and supersedes without another model call.

The graph took under a second to build and resolved every explicit cross-reference in the test library, so the agent could follow links instead of rediscovering connections on each question.

The graph’s job is evidence navigation, not modeling everything the organization knows. The wiki still provides the synthesis. Unlike an extraction-heavy knowledge graph pipeline, this layer reuses existing references and citations rather than extracting and reconciling entities with a model. Construction requires no additional model calls, though edges derived from the wiki still depend on the accuracy of its model-generated citations.

Two tools let the agent navigate the map: locate finds a starting point that matches the question, and expand follows its connections to supporting passages and related documents. Where there’s only one path, expand follows it automatically; where the path branches, the agent chooses where to go next. This pattern of locating relevant nodes and gathering connected context also appears in GraphRAG systems such as Microsoft’s GraphRAG.

@tool(parse_docstring=True)
async def locate(terms: str, within: str | None = None) -> dict:
    """Find where to start: match the question's words against document titles,
    section headings, wiki pages, and claim statements."""
    ...

@tool(parse_docstring=True)
async def expand(node: str, edges: list[str] | None = None, hops: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Open one node and list its typed edges (cites, refers_to, supersedes,
    amends, attaches_to, and their inverses). With hops > 1 and one edge type,
    walk that edge while there is a single path, and stop at a branch."""
    ...

Better accuracy, lower cost, faster answers

Adding explicit evidence paths improved every measure over the wiki alone. Accuracy rose 27%, citation consistency doubled, median answer time fell 40% , and cost per correct answer fell 58%. The evidence graph complemented the wiki’s context with more directed retrieval, improving both accuracy and consistency without making the agent fully deterministic.

When is adding memory worth the cost?

The strongest case for a compiled wiki is repeated cross-source reasoning. In our experiment, the wiki helped the agent apply domain relationships rather than reconstruct them through search. But the memory layer alone didn’t make evidence retrieval consistent. Adding explicit graph edges improved citation consistency and accuracy while reducing retrieval work.

The wiki provided a strong foundation for a lightweight evidence graph, derived deterministically from its existing citations and document references. This let us add explicit evidence paths without additional model calls or the need to model everything the organization knows.

Whether a wiki is worth the investment depends on reuse. Our reported answer costs exclude compilation, and adding documents cost about $0.09 each. Ingestion and ongoing maintenance may outweigh retrieval savings for simple lookups, where search alone was just as accurate and faster, especially at enterprise scale.

The tradeoff changes when multiple agents repeatedly answer questions spanning the same disconnected sources. A shared wiki preserves the relationships between those sources, while graph edges guide agents to supporting evidence. In our tests, that combination produced more accurate answers at a lower cost per correct answer. With enough reuse, savings from avoiding repeated context reconstruction can offset the cost of building and maintaining memory.

What's next

Next, we want to build wikis more dynamically, compiling and retaining only the context agents need for cross-source questions rather than entire repositories.

We also want to explore claims and typed edges as a foundation for other kinds of agent memory. Linking knowledge to evidence and detecting when it changes could help ground semantic memory (facts), episodic memory (what happened), and procedural memory (how to do things).

Want to add wikis into your agents? Check out our OpenWiki resources:

  • Openwiki Documentation
  • OpenWiki Code Repository

Acknowledgments

Thank you Colin Francis and Nick Hollon for their thoughts around OpenWiki and evaluations!

Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
items.summary:
This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one [...]

Read More...

The post Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval.
  • In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system).
  • For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook.

Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. 

Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale.

Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval

The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. 

Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. 

Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture 

Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs.

New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale 

The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline.

Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits 

With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motivated a joint collaboration with NVIDIA.

Each of these challenges drove a corresponding advance.

Unlocking Retrieval Performance Through Model-System Co-Design

Next-Gen Retrieval Model Architecture — Retrieval Mixture-of-Experts 

The latest iteration of Meta Andromeda introduces three synergistic architectural innovations that bring large language model (LLM)-inspired mixture-of-experts (MoE) into the retrieval (see Figure 1). With this highly expressive yet inference-efficient architecture, a new retrieval performance-efficiency Pareto frontier has been established: model performance approaches ranking-level in a typical retrieval-then-ranking system, at approximately 300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval model.

On the user modeling side, we transitioned from a single user tower to an ensemble of specialized user towers as experts. This captures diverse, time-evolving, and contextualized user interests by integrating a vast array of high-fidelity signals: sequential ad engagement events, user-cohort representations, LLM-derived semantic features, and cross-surface co-engagement signals.

In the candidate ads tower, we employ a joint encoding strategy that incorporates real-time serving context, ensuring that downstream interaction models receive context-aware representations.

In the interaction overarch layer, the interaction model evolved from dense neural networks into an MoE attention-based gating network that dynamically routes candidates across the most relevant user experts, delivering near-ranking-level performance at a fraction of the FLOPs.

A defining property of the new architecture is that its performance is co-designed with the underlying hardware execution model. Model inference throughput has reached over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200 GPU, and this efficiency allows model capacity to grow further, through richer feature interactions, additional expert sub-networks, and deeper architectures, without a proportional increase in GPU cost. Each incremental model advancement translates into greater advertiser value.

 

Co-Designing the Model and System Onto a Single GPU Pipeline

The 2026 Meta Andromeda pushes the model-system co-design to the next level with two innovations — a single GPU kernel fusing both model and system workloads per user-ad interaction and a strategy to co-locate per user request logics with per user-ad GPU kernels in a single GPU box. To this end, a highly optimized and fully fused GPU pipeline is built to host the entire end-to-end Meta Andromeda workflow.

Fused Kernel

At a high level, Meta Andromeda’s inference time per user-ad workload is a compact sequence of operations across model execution and system logics — gathering embeddings, executing user-ad interaction models, and scoring. The ~300x FLOPs reduction in the retrieval MoE gating architecture creates the necessary headroom and is less resistant to fully fuse both model execution and non-model system workloads into a single GPU kernel, compared to the 2024 launch where only operations within the model execution were fused. Consequently, the fused kernel now runs at over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200.

This matters because retrieval workloads are fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. At billions of ads per second, even a small intermediate tensor per ad multiplies into terabytes per second of high bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. The memory workload of these intermediate tensors, not arithmetic, becomes the dominant bottleneck in multi-kernel retrieval pipelines.

The fused kernel eliminates this bottleneck entirely. Rather than dispatching multiple small GPU kernels for model and system operations, it executes the entire per user-ad computation in one pass. Intermediate results stay in GPU registers and thread block shared memory and are never materialized to HBM, achieving high utilization of the GPU’s peak memory bandwidth rather than wasting it on redundant intermediate traffic. 

Co-Location Strategy

Measured in isolation, the per user-ad fused kernel runs at multi-billion ads per second on a single GPU. However, per-user request operations such as the index matching (i.e., enforcing advertisers’ targeting rules) and top-K selection run on separate local CPU hosts and communicate with the fused GPU kernel scoring service on remote accelerators through the network connection. At multi-billion ads per second throughput, this traffic alone saturates the network link, making the network bandwidth become the bottleneck rather than GPU compute.

The co-design response was to collapse the system architecture to match the model architecture: co-locate index matching, scoring, and top-K selection on the same GPU. Instead of shipping large candidate lists across hosts, the system sends a compact request payload — user features and a targeting query — to a single GPU server, which runs the entire retrieval pipeline locally and returns only the final top-K results. This reduces network traffic by ~100x and shifts the system back to a GPU-compute-bound regime.

Moving index matching onto the GPU is not straightforward. Ads index matching evaluates complex advertiser-defined targeting logic across tens of feature categories, and must support real-time index updates as ads are created, modified, or expired throughout the day. Supporting this on GPU required redesigning the index structure for GPU-parallel execution while preserving the full fidelity of production targeting semantics.

A Single GPU Pipeline for Meta Andromeda

Combining the aforementioned two innovations, the fully co-located single GPU pipeline processes over one billion ads per second on a single GPU server while scoring every eligible ad in the candidate pool. This is a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models, and as the next section describes, significant headroom remains.

GPU-Accelerated Retrieval: The Meta-NVIDIA Collaboration

With the production pipeline running at over one billion ads per second, a natural question follows: How close is the system to the ceiling of the current generation hardware, and how much headroom remains for future model growth? In early 2026, Meta and NVIDIA launched a joint collaboration to answer this question — systematically optimizing each component of the retrieval pipeline to push throughput toward hardware limits. NVIDIA contributed optimized GPU kernels, and Meta integrated and benchmarked the full pipeline. Each component achieved 2x to 5x speedup over the baseline.

Interaction Network (Retrieval MoE Gating Network)

The optimized gating kernel improved by 5.3x, from 2.4 billion to over 10 billion ads per second, reaching ~85% of the GPU’s peak HBM bandwidth. At this throughput, the execution time / latency of the gating mechanism is just as fast as what a simple dot-product scoring kernel achieves on the same hardware — while the model is substantially more expressive. This is the co-design validation: the additional model complexity is essentially free on Tensor Core hardware. INT8 quantization achieved a further up to 2x throughput increase over the optimized FP16 kernels, with accuracy on par with 16-bit precision.

Index Matching

Through targeted GPU kernel optimizations, index matching throughput improved over 2x, reaching over 100 billion ads per second — an order of magnitude higher than the scoring network. This headroom means index matching can be re-run across multiple retrieval pathways without becoming a bottleneck.

End-to-End GPU Pipeline

Beyond individual kernels, the collaboration profiled the full retrieval flow and identified that data movement between pipeline components — not computation — accounted for a significant fraction of end-to-end latency. By co-designing data layouts across index matching and scoring to eliminate unnecessary indirection, the team removed this overhead. With all optimizations applied, the full pipeline benchmarks at multiple times the current production throughput on a single GPU server, with further gains expected as additional optimizations integrate into production.

Continuing Work on Next-Generation NVIDIA Platforms

Building on the Hopper results above, we are extending our optimization and co-design work to Grace Blackwell. Here, we are focusing on platform design optimizations that enable different CPU-to-GPU compute ratios, which our work so far suggests is an important factor for Andromeda-like workloads. We are evaluating how sensitive end-to-end application performance is to these ratios, using Grace-class CPU performance and Blackwell-class GPU performance for their respective parts of the workload.

More broadly, we are exploring how these findings extend to the next platform generation, where greater flexibility in CPU+GPU execution, resource ratios, and coupling could bring more of these architectural improvements to bear on Andromeda-like workloads.

These results confirm that the co-designed retrieval pipeline is not yet at its ceiling. With quantization unlocking further scoring throughput and index matching operating at an order of magnitude above the scoring network, the architecture is positioned to absorb significantly more model complexity — deeper interaction networks, richer feature spaces, and additional retrieval pathways — without proportional infrastructure growth.

The Path Forward for Ads Retrieval

The advances described here follow a single principle: The largest gains come from designing model, system, and hardware as one integrated stack, rather than optimizing each in isolation. The retrieval MoE gating architecture delivers near-ranking-level expressiveness at no additional serving cost. Fusing the entire retrieval pipeline onto a single GPU eliminates network and memory bottlenecks. And pushing the pipeline towards its hardware ceiling confirms substantial headroom remains.

Looking ahead, the co-design principle that drove these results applies equally to next-generation model architectures and hardware platforms, with the demonstrated headroom enabling continued scaling without proportional infrastructure growth.

For people who use Meta’s products, this translates directly into better ads that are more relevant to them, delivered within the same latency budget. For advertisers, it means better customer matches and more conversions. For Meta, it means increased business from advertisers and lower costs, as each GPU now evaluates more ads per second. As the volume of eligible ads continues to grow, driven by Advantage+ automation and generative AI creative tools, Meta Andromeda’s co-designed architecture scales to meet it.

items.title: Thin, Light and Built for Everything: NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows Laptops Gain New Models, Agent Tools and Games
items.summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified […]
items.content:
NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do.

RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere.

New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include:

  • NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark. 
  • The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support. 
  • Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents.
  • Phantom Blade Zero, S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5.
  • Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark.

Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe

Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages.

Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to:

  • “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.”
  • “Translate this audio into English.”
  • “List what decisions were made in this meeting.”

Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware.

It’s available today on Hugging Face in the BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 formats, and offers flexible deployment options for developers with support on NVIDIA RTX Spark, DGX Spark systems and Jetson AGX Thor devices. Developers can deploy NVFP4 versions through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM.

Learn more in the NVIDIA technical blog.

Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources

On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment.

With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App, users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. 

Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings.

Liquid AI: One Model Family, Many Ways to Work

Liquid AI’s LFM3 provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model.

These models support local workflows such as agents running in Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw to triage inboxes and manage calendars, read documents and app screens, transcribe and translate speech, answer spoken questions about handwritten math, and route support tickets or voice requests. 

Developers can run LFM3 models on RTX Spark with native support through llama.cpp and vLLM, and fine-tune the models locally.

‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches With DLSS 4.5

S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches tonight, Oct. 28, at 7 p.m. PT on Steam and the Epic Games Store. Players can take on the role of Soul, a swordsman framed for his master’s murder, as he travels the martial world to uncover a conspiracy.

NVIDIA worked with S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing to add ray-traced effects to the title. On RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX GPU-powered PCs, ray tracing adds more accurate bounced lighting, detailed reflections and realistic shadows on foliage and terrain. The NVIDIA DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation feature boosts frame rates with up to 6x frame generation, or adjusts the multiplier on the fly to hit a player’s target frame rate.

Read more on GeForce.com.

RTX Remix Breathes New Life Into Classics 

NVIDIA RTX Remix, the modding platform for remastering classic games with path tracing and DLSS, released version 1.6 last week. This update brought RTX Remix to the world’s largest gaming community: Minecraft. Both creators and players can render Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1 through RTX Remix with DLSS-accelerated path tracing and take full advantage of realistic lighting and materials in their future creations.

The update also adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, up to 6x Multi Frame Generation, native RTX Spark support and agent-assisted workflows. Starting today, those upgrades come to Portal with RTX and the Half-Life 2 RTX demo. Both now support RTX Spark, with DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering for more lifelike lighting and materials, a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation and new options that speed up path tracing. 

RTX Remix 1.6 also makes AI-powered modding simpler. A redesigned ComfyUI workflow lets modders generate physically based materials directly inside RTX Remix, with no application programming interface setup, batch processing for full projects and presets for less technical creators. Plus, with NVIDIA agent skills, compatible AI agents can work directly with RTX Remix to help speed up remastering projects.

Learn more in the RTX Remix blog. 

RTX Spark Laptops: Beautifully Designed, Built for Everything

RTX Spark laptops come in a range of designs, so users can choose one that fits how they work and play. Options include different screen sizes, colors, touchscreens, pen support and two-in-one convertibles. RTX Spark laptops are as thin as 14mm and as light as three pounds, with all-day battery life.

Such slim designs are possible because RTX Spark places the GPU, CPU and up to 128GB of unified memory on one power-efficient superchip. Creative projects and AI models draw from the same memory pool, so a laptop can take on work that used to call for a desktop workstation, even when unplugged. 

Here’s what this means for:

  • AI developers: Run models and agents locally on NVIDIA CUDA — the same platform that powers AI in the cloud — with a path to deploy across more than 150 million NVIDIA RTX AI PCs and NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud.
  • Creators: RTX Spark can edit camera native 4:2:2 video and render 3D scenes of up to 90GB. Adobe Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases.
  • Gamers: Hundreds of games run on RTX Spark, with NVIDIA DLSS, ray tracing, Reflex and G-SYNC delivering sharper visuals and smoother, more responsive gameplay.

RTX Spark laptops are available now from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI, starting at $2,599, with 128GB configurations on shelves. Find a laptop on the RTX Spark product page.

#ICYMI: More Updates From NVIDIA Local AI

Microducks learn to walk with help from RTX Spark: During the GTC Berlin keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed how AI agents running on RTX Spark can help train Hugging Face’s Microduck robot. A new NVIDIA technical blog walks through the workflow: Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt plan an obstacle course on RTX Spark, Astra builds the 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Lab trains the navigation policy and RTX Spark validates it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Watch the demo and try the playbook.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available, enabling natural conversations and multistep agent tasks with as little as 4GB of memory. The model powers local voice assistants, game characters and embedded interfaces on RTX Spark, DGX Spark, GeForce RTX GPUs and NVIDIA Jetson devices. It supports llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio, and works with Hermes and OpenClaw. For more demanding agent workloads, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run local agents on RTX Spark.

Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6-billion-parameter open weights model that lets users generate and edit images locally. NVIDIA-optimized versions run on RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM. Developers can also fine-tune the model on RTX Spark using an NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel recipe to customize it for specific creative workflows.

NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB is now available to purchase from manufacturer partners, giving developers and researchers another way to build and run AI locally. Powered by the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, it combines 64GB of unified memory with DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack for agent development, inference and fine-tuning. Learn more and explore purchase options.

Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter. Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X.

items.title: Why aren’t you building proactive agents yet?
items.summary:
Ever hear of the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon? It's when you learn a word for the first time, and suddenly start hearing it everywhere. I think the same principle applies in software engineering: You learn about a simple, but effective, design pattern, and then suddenly start seeing it everywhere.

We're seeing this happen with proactive agents, where we've noticed that nearly all of your favorite emerging proactive agentic systems are powered by a very simple mechanism: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case.

The future belongs to proactive, always-on, ambient agents. Launches like Muse, Instinct, Dots, Claude Duet, Hone, and more reflect this.

Crons power a few different capabilities that combine to make these agents proactive, personalized, and ambient — that is, they can perform tasks on their own, without being manually instructed.

In this blog, we will go through the capabilities that crons unlock, the two core underlying parts you need in order to build agents like this, and then show examples of how you can do this in Managed Deep Agents.

We’ve seen the impact crons can have. Proactivity is the new default for agent behaviour because of the breadth of new functions it unlocks. More than 70% of Managed Deepagent runs on LangSmith come from scheduled runs rather than a human typing a message.

What do crons unlock?

Crons, despite being a simple concept, unlock a few different behaviors that shape these proactive, always-on agents.

Memory: A distinctive part of all these agents is that they remember facts about you over longer time horizons. Implementing this partially involves running a background job to condense previous conversations into a denser form of memory. This is colloquially called “dreaming”. Under the hood, this is just a cron that runs on some cadence (e.g. once a day) and updates long-term memory with any learnings from reflecting on the conversations.

Proactiveness: Part of what makes these agents work is that they initiate communication about an idea that they think you may be interested in. Under the hood, the way that this works is there is some “idea” of what this agent should be accomplishing.

For a general purpose agent, it may be as simple as being a good assistant: taking steps to anticipate what you need next, like flagging an upcoming deadline, following up on an open thread, or surfacing news related to your work. For specialized agents, like with Hone, the agent is working towards an explicit goal. The cron then runs on some cadence (once an hour) and prompts the agent to explore new actions to progress on its goal. These actions then show up as proactive messages to the user.

Smart Triage: There is so much noise in the world. A big use case for always-on agents is to monitor a source of information (Slack, Email, etc) and ping the user with relevant messages. Under the hood, this can be implemented as a cron that runs on a cadence (once every ten minutes) and is prompting an agent to look at an event stream and notify the user of anything of note.

Follow ups: Crons aren’t just used in the background. Oftentimes users may ask to be reminded about something at some point. Crons can be used to set a schedule to wake up and remind the user then.

Orchestration: Agent fleets can be managed by a single orchestration agent with the ability to wake itself up in the future. An orchestrator agent can monitor a fleet with crons. It can sleep while waiting for an asynchronous subtask to finish, and wake itself back up again to check in on progress at regular intervals.

The two key parts to building proactive agents

In order two build these types of agents, we’ve found that there is generally two key parts.

First is a robust cron server. You will need a server that makes it easy for developers to add crons . They should be able to add them with whatever schedule they need, and include a prompt to run as part of that. If the agent needs certain skills or permissions when running, these should be included. If there are a lot of runs at a specific time point, the server should “jitter” them slightly to spread out the load.

Second, you need an agent-friendly interface. For actions like follow ups, the agent needs to be able to interact with these reminders. It needs an easy - but governed - way to set up and modify reminders.

Build this with MDA

Managed Deep Agents - which are hosted using LangSmith Deployments - provide a built-in cron server that can dynamically trigger an agent run. A scheduled run is deceptively simple: It is just the prompt that was passed in, triggered at a schedule, with the thread and memory based on the principal who created the schedule. This toolkit above provides foundation for tools that accept only a prompt and a cron schedule.

With Managed Deep Agents, schedules can be defined either statically or dynamically by an agent.

For example, building an agent with a fixed schedule as part of its core design - say, a daily sales readout - is just a file in schedules/:

# schedules/daily_digest.py
from managed_deepagents import define_schedule

schedule = define_schedule(
    cron="0 8 * * 1-5",
    timezone="America/Los_Angeles",
    prompt="Inspect the sales report using your tools and send a KPI readout.",
)

Managed Deep Agents also offers dynamic schedules, where end users can prompt your agent to schedule recurring tasks that you didn’t anticipate in development. To support this, wrap the Schedules SDK in tools:

# tools/scheduling.py
from langchain.tools import tool
from managed_deepagents import ManagedDeepAgentRuntime


@tool
async def set_schedule(prompt: str, cron: str, runtime: ManagedDeepAgentRuntime) -> str:
    """Run a prompt for the current user on a cron schedule."""
    item = await runtime.schedules.create(owner={"type": "user"}, cron=cron, prompt=prompt)
    return f"Created schedule {item['id']}."


@tool
async def list_schedules(runtime: ManagedDeepAgentRuntime) -> str:
    """List the current user's schedules."""
    page = await runtime.schedules.list(owner={"type": "user"})
    return str(page["items"])


@tool
async def delete_schedule(schedule_id: str, runtime: ManagedDeepAgentRuntime) -> str:
    """Delete one of the current user's schedules."""
    await runtime.schedules.delete(schedule_id, owner={"type": "user"})
    return f"Deleted schedule {schedule_id}."

‍Developers need flexibility, and the Managed Deep Agents tool system is designed with this in mind. Different agent types may need to expose different toolkits for scheduling. In some cases, a basic remind_me wrapping one-off run or a check_in_later may be sufficient:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from langchain.tools import tool
from managed_deepagents import ManagedDeepAgentRuntime


@tool
async def check_in_later(prompt: str, minutes: int, runtime: ManagedDeepAgentRuntime) -> str:
    """Run a prompt once for the current user, a number of minutes from now."""
    at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=minutes)
    item = await runtime.schedules.create(owner={"type": "user"}, at=at, prompt=prompt)
    return f"Scheduled a check-in {item['id']}."

Get started with adding schedules to your Managed Deep Agents from our documentation: langch.in/mda. You’re one mda init and mda deploy away from distributing a proactive agent within your organization.

‍

items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub, such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid
  • Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
  • Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
  • Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
  • Fixed per-directory and paths: skills not being found after a Bash cd deeper into a git repository
  • Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
  • Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave claude -p with no output
  • Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
  • Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
  • Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit
