items.title: How We Built Our Design Agent
items.summary:
• Taste comes from context. Models already write good code, but they need your designers’ principles, guardrails against AI slop, and the reasoning behind feedback to make work that looks like yours.
  • Give the agent a designer’s computer. Every Slack thread gets its own sandbox where the agent keeps the project between turns, works across a video engine, image tools, and a shared canvas, and inspects its own renders.
  • Delete rules when the model improves. Rules that make up for a model’s weaknesses expire, so keep the design principles and remove the workarounds as models get better.
  • Long-running agents need multiplayer UX. Big jobs run for hours on async subagents, so the Slack thread shows the plan, live progress, and an approval before anything ships, and anyone on the team can steer the agent mid-run.
  • You can fork it. The open-source repo has the full harness, and Managed Deep Agents deploys it to your team’s Slack.

‍

The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code.

Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents. It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great.

So how did we go from such low quality to this?

We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company.

This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film.

We've open-sourced our design agent. Fork the open-source repo, add your brand tokens, fonts and skills, and deploy it to your team's Slack with Managed Deep Agents.

Then join us at GTM Engineering Live on October 28. We'll go under the hood of the harness and the UX, and show the work that didn't fit in this post.

Building a design agent for scale

LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work.

To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things:

  1. Our designers' expert judgment, written into the agent's skills and checks so it knows what good looks like.
  2. A custom environment around the model, including a video editing computer with tools for every layer of the design work.
  3. The right UX, so a whole team can collaborate on a project that runs for hours from one Slack thread.

Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox, integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing.

Key results

  • Content Studio has delivered over 3,000 assets across the company, including more than 80 slide decks. One of its decks was even used in our most-watched organic YouTube video.
  • Posts with its work drew about 4.5M views on X.
  • On the LangChain account, posts with its visuals have earned about 2x the likes and 3.7x the bookmarks of other posts.
  • Three in four requests now come from outside marketing, and 75% of users are repeat visitors who come back every week.
  • The median request now costs about 50 cents in model spend, down from about $8 in mid-September. Our own code shrank by about 80% after the migration to Managed Deep Agents.

Is AI actually good at design?

Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design?

The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence”. The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. Familiar isn’t always bad, but we wanted our agent to make choices that followed its purpose.

Katie Dill, Head of Design at Stripe, makes a helpful comparison. Under pressure to build quickly after World War II, builders copied the clean shapes and bare surfaces of modernism over and over. The copies kept the look while losing the thought and character behind it. Her warning is that AI can do the same to software. She calls it “zombie UI” and says we need a point of view, because “if you don’t, AI will give it for you.”

We don't think AI is bad at design. It just doesn't have a point of view unless you provide it, and giving it ours meant teaching it our taste.

Teaching a design agent taste

Taste is the judgment that separates work that's correct from work that's good. In design, two layouts can use the right fonts, colors and spacing, and only one of them makes its point. Taste comes from what Dill calls "getting really good at noticing."

That noticing is how we learned to spot AI slop, which most often shows up when a brief leaves a decision to the agent.

For example, the image on the left below was created by a local coding agent with our brand skill (which includes colors, fonts, logos, etc.). But the final result missed critical components, such as the correct logo lockup, text alignment, and which colors were our primary vs. secondary brand colors.

The same prompt produced a perfectly on-brand image in Content Studio. This happened because the local agent filled in each decision that the brief didn't cover with what it had seen most. With this methodology, Content Studio filled the same gaps with our choices.

The guidelines we gave Content Studio started with the basics, including color tokens, font weights, spacing, and alignment. But much of the improvement came from what we added on top. We introduced design principles, like having one focal point per frame, guardrails against common AI design patterns, and the reasoning behind each piece of feedback. Combined with better underlying models, these helped Content Studio learn to think and communicate more like a designer.

It didn't start that way. In one of our early motion graphics, a bird flies off screen with a ribbon of light trailing behind it for less than a second. We asked for no sharp edges, but the first pass came back clunky, with harsh, rounded edges. A designer would have understood what we meant. The edges should soften, while the tail tapers and fades in the direction opposite the bird's movement.

By a later iteration, the agent was evaluating that detail with a designer's eye. Using a quick sketch to identify where the bird's tail should be, it built its own frame-by-frame check to ensure the ribbon stayed attached. Most viewers would never notice the detail consciously, but they'd feel it if something was off.

The measurable problems were the easiest to solve. Default capitalization used to come up frequently in reviews, but an automated check now catches every instance. The harder decisions are more subjective, like whether a campaign idea is strong enough, the message comes through clearly, or the execution resonates with the audience. When a designer makes one of those calls, we capture the reasoning in a skill so the agent can apply it to future drafts.

Content Studio changed who can do design work. A PM, engineer, or founder can brief the agent in Slack and walk away with something on brand and ready to ship. Three in four requests now come from outside marketing. For designers, the role has shifted closer to that of a creative director, setting the direction and reviewing the work rather than producing every asset themselves.

Getting the design judgment right was one part of the process. We also needed to give the agent the tools and environment to execute on it.

Building a media harness

A designer works across several tools, from Photoshop for stills and a video engine for motion to a shared canvas for prototyping and collaboration. They also rely on brand guidelines, design assets, and company documentation.

An agent needs a similar setup, with a computer to work on, tools for different parts of the design process, and the context a designer brings to their work. The harness brings these pieces together. Deep Agents provides the underlying harness, including the agent loop, planning, files, subagents, and context management. Managed Deep Agents packages and runs it in production. We built the environment around it, giving the agent a computer where it can maintain a project, work across tools, and inspect the results.

harness_v1

Our first version of that harness tried to do the designing for the model. The early models needed a lot of help to make a motion graphic or a launch film we'd want to ship. To compensate for what they couldn't yet figure out themselves, our intuition was to put more of our own design judgment into instructions and code.

So, we built a design system with 115 reusable UI components for titles, layouts, and animations, along with guidance on when and how to use them. This gave the model a set of existing designs to work from, reducing the number of creative decisions it had to make from scratch.

That helped it stay on brand, but the agent would just repeat the same layouts and animations for each frame without much variety:

We knew the models would eventually be great at this task, so we kept building the environment for that moment, experimenting with the skills and tooling along the way. Sometimes we'd add more references or more detailed instructions to help the model. Other times we'd remove them entirely and see what it could do on its own.

But the results still weren't where we wanted them, and closing the gap required increasingly more engineering work. We kept adding rules to the skills, writing more motion code, and building more components to compensate for what the model couldn't do.

Then Opus 5.5 arrived, and we saw an immediate jump in quality. We revisited the skills and removed most of the hard-coded rules, keeping the design principles and high-level guidance. The results improved further, with more variety and less repetition. The model was finally making creative decisions we'd previously tried to prebuild for it.

This was our Bitter Lesson. Rules designed to compensate for a model's weaknesses become less useful as models improve. What lasts is the environment around the model, including the tools it uses, the context it draws from, and how people guide its work. Instead of prebuilding creative decisions, we focused on making the harness flexible enough to take advantage of each new generation of models.

Designer’s computer

To show the harness in action, we asked Content Studio to make a film about how it works with a video project end to end. The result stars a parrot in a pixel jungle narrated in the style of David Attenborough (voiced with ElevenLabs). Let's use it to walk through the layers of the harness: computer, tools and context behind its work.

Design is iterative. You make something, look at it and change it, often many times. So the agent needs a computer it can keep working on across a whole conversation. Each Slack thread gets its own LangSmith Sandbox, an isolated Linux machine with a filesystem and a shell, and the project lives there for the life of the thread.

Everything the agent creates is built with code, whether it's an HTML page for a slide, a data spec for a chart, or an animation timeline for a video. This makes it easy to iterate without starting over. If someone asks to bring the parrot in earlier, the agent can change a single timing value and render again without affecting the artwork or copy. With a flat image or generated video clip, even a small edit could mean recreating the entire asset.

The brief, plan, scene code, audio and renders all live in one project folder, which every subagent on the job works from.

On top of that, we installed the tools a designer would reach for at each layer of the work:

Motion is the most difficult layer. It runs on two engines:

  1. HyperFrames for editing: HyperFrames, HeyGen's open-source video framework, turns a video into a web page. Clips, screen recordings, captions and text are just elements on that page, and a GSAP timeline moves them around. So when someone asks to caption a webinar or cut a product demo, the agent edits it like a web page. Its CLI is basically the agent's editing suite: lint the composition, pull a frame to check, render the cut. We also install HeyGen's official skills, so the agent learns the format from the people who built it.
  2. motion-studio for animation: A web page can't blur fast motion, make things glow or turn a logo in 3D, and that's the finish we wanted for original animation. So we built our own canvas engine. The agent writes code that draws every pixel of every frame, and the engine blends up to 16 moments into each one, the same way a camera shutter blurs movement. The parrot film was made this way.

Both engines render each frame based on its timestamp, so a frame at ten seconds looks the same regardless of when it's rendered. This lets the agent inspect individual moments without rendering the entire film, while also allowing us to render multiple frames in parallel. Audio runs on the same timeline, keeping narration, music, and sound effects synchronized with the visuals.

With this setup, the agent can create almost anything. But without further guidance, it defaults to the model's own design choices rather than ours. The next challenge was teaching it to work within our brand and design standards.

Designer's brain

We organized the agent's knowledge around four distinct functions, each with a clear purpose. Skills guide how to perform specific tasks, while the wiki provides context about our company and what good work looks like. Anything measurable is handled by a gate, a deterministic check written in code. A separate memory layer captures what people teach the agent over time.

Skills

The first thing the agent does with a request is work out what kind of job it is. That's handled by our media-production skill. We call it a router skill because most of it is one table. Each row maps a kind of ask (a campaign, a restyle, a thumbnail, a post, a YouTube package, a launch film, a short animation) to the path and the specialist skill that handle it. The router also decides whether the work needs a shared visual canvas, and it keeps small edits out of the full process.

For a film like the one above, the router picks the launch-film skill designed for directing a large motion production. Each of our 48 skills, close to 1,000 files in all, is scoped to a job rather than a topic, so its description reads like a routing rule, including when not to use it.

Skills compose instead of repeating each other. launch-film directs and motion-studio makes the picture and sound, so the craft of animation is written once. launch-film also carries role briefs for the subagents it will start, and a case study of a real 88-second launch film we rebuilt shot for shot in code. That case study is where the agent learned how to split a film between subagents. It cuts at hard scene changes, keeps a continuous camera move with one subagent, and freezes shared code before anyone works in parallel.

Descriptions matter for tools just as much as for skills. To keep context usage down, we put MCP tools behind a built-in search. The agent starts with only our own tools and loads additional tool schemas as needed, using keyword searches across tool names and descriptions.

Wiki

Skills explain how to do a job, while the wiki provides the context and reference material needed to do it well. It covers everything from brand tokens, graphic language, and voice to platforms, campaigns, and product information. A dedicated motion wiki covers directing, craft, sound, and review, alongside breakdowns of 70 reference films.

Rather than duplicating this information across skills, we link directly to the wiki. This keeps shared knowledge in one place and makes updates easier. When something like a font rule changes, we only need to update it once, and every skill can reference the latest version.

Knowing how we work doesn't necessarily make motion design cheaper. A wrong creative decision can still cost hours of rendering.

Spec-driven design

Motion is especially expensive to get wrong, both in render time and tokens. A storyboard frame takes about 50 milliseconds to render, compared to 8 to 40 seconds for a single second of finished film. With subagents writing, rendering, and reviewing every act, those costs add up quickly. So the agent develops ideas in the storyboard first, where it can explore different directions cheaply, before moving into full production once a direction is approved.

To support that exploration, we gave the agent a library of reference films to draw inspiration from, much like a designer working from a mood board. When it can't find the right look, it uses an image model to generate new references, starting with quick drafts before refining the most promising options. These images help establish the visual direction, while the storyboard and final film are still built in code using real typography and brand assets.

Once we pick a direction, the approved storyboard becomes the spec the rest of the film is built against. Then the project moves through three stages:

  1. A storyboard, to agree on the visual idea, the copy and the shots.
  2. An animatic, a rough cut timed to the audio, to check the pacing that stills can't show.
  3. Production, where subagents build, check and render the approved shots.

We first described this order in the skill's instructions, and the agent sometimes skipped a review to save time. Now the pipeline enforces it in code, so assembly waits until every act passes review, while the instructions still guide the creative calls. The order that must always hold lives in code, and the judgment stays in the prompt.

Point, don’t prompt

Picking between those directions is a team decision. Slack works well for asking for work and receiving it, but a thread is linear text and a storyboard is spatial, so feedback ends up describing where something is instead of pointing at it, and every change, even a one-word fix, has to go back through the agent as a new prompt.

Paper solved this for us. It's a design canvas built with agents in mind, with an MCP server that gives the agent direct control over the file. People can work in that same file, comparing directions side by side, leaving comments on specific frames, or making edits themselves. Because the canvas is shared, the agent can return to the file and use those comments and edits to guide its next iteration.

The challenge was that Paper's agent tools only run inside its desktop app, while our agent operates in a cloud sandbox. To bridge that gap, we run Paper Desktop headlessly on an always-on Linux worker, using a virtual display and an authenticated bridge to connect the two. A single setup supports the entire team.

Even after approval, turning a storyboard into a finished film can take hours. By that point, the work resembles a small project, with multiple pieces being built in parallel that need to come together. Coordinating all of this is more than a single agent turn can handle.

Agent as a chief of staff

Consider the parrot film from earlier, midway through production in Slack. One person shares a reference, another suggests a different opening, and a third leaves feedback on frame four, all while the agent is still building. It's like a brainstorm where the person taking notes is also responsible for making the film. Synchronous subagents don't work well here because the main agent has to wait for them to finish, leaving no way for people to interact with it in the meantime.

To solve this, we made subagents asynchronous and shifted the main agent's role from implementer to chief of staff. It breaks complex projects into smaller, isolated tasks, assigns them to subagents, and runs the work in parallel. Meanwhile, it keeps the team informed as things change, so people can continue giving feedback and steering the project.

For each task, the main agent creates a subagent profile with a clear brief covering its role, relevant context, file ownership, and how to validate the work. It also selects the model and effort level based on the complexity of the task.

We also added a small set of tools for the main agent to coordinate work:

  • start_task hands a part to a subagent in the background
  • check_tasks shows what's running and reads finished reports
  • cancel_task and resume_task stop work that no longer fits the brief, or pick it up where it left off
  • report_progress lets a subagent send updates mid-job
  • schedule_wakeup gives the main agent a timer to trigger another run and continue the job

Under the hood, each subagent is the ordinary Deep Agents task tool running as a background task. When it finishes, our code queues a new run of the main agent carrying the result. People can also steer the main agent mid-run, since a message that arrives while it's working is inserted before its next model call. The subagents coordinate through the project folder, each writing only the files it owns and keeping its progress on disk.

With the work running in the background, the thread has to show what's happening. The main agent keeps it up to date with a plan and ETA, a live status line with running subagents, render progress and spend, an acknowledgment for each edit, and an approval card before anything goes public.

One of the clearest tests of this approach came from an overnight job to reskin a 52-slide presentation. The agent started by creating three sample slides and reviewing its own work before moving through the rest of the deck in numbered batches for approval. It also added two new slides along the way. Overnight, the main agent ran for about an hour while its subagents collectively worked for more than six hours, all without blocking the conversation.

The self-improving harness

A designer who's worked with a team for months learns its preferences and doesn't need to hear the same feedback twice. Without memory, the agent would start from scratch with every new thread. To avoid this, we built two learning loops. The fast loop captures feedback as people give it, while the slow loop learns from completed projects in the background.

The fast loop: When someone shares a rule or preference, the agent saves it in the same turn. Managed Deep Agents stores memory as plain files in two layers, one shared across the team and another specific to each person.

Personal preferences carry across threads, but shared standards take precedence, and anything created for a company channel follows the company voice. Each layer has an AGENTS.md file that loads with every model call. We now limit these files to a 200-line index after an early version grew to 500K tokens.

The slow loop: After each job, our learn_from_job tool launches a lightweight subagent that captures up to five evidence-backed lessons and associates them with the skill used. Future jobs read and rate those lessons, and once a week, a background agent incorporates the ones that prove useful into the skills and wiki.

What’s next

Remember those early reviews? The biggest improvement came from capturing our designers’ judgment in a shared environment the agent could learn from, rather than leaving it scattered across review threads. In the process, we made design work accessible to more people.

Next, we want the agent to manage the entire campaign lifecycle, and some of that is already working. It publishes company social posts through Buffer once an authorized approver signs off, drafts posts for employees to share from their own accounts, and runs scheduled routines, including a daily review that suggests posts worth quoting.

Our goal is to take this further, so a single approved creative direction can carry an entire campaign from one thread. The agent would write the brief, create assets for each channel, schedule posts, help the team amplify them, and use performance data to inform the next campaign. People would still review and approve everything before it goes public.

Build your own design agent: The open-source repo has the harness from this post: the sandbox computer, skills, wiki and memory, async subagents and the Slack UX. Fork it, add your brand tokens, fonts and skills, and deploy it to your team's Slack with Managed Deep Agents.

Then join us at GTM Engineering Live on October 28. We'll go under the hood of the harness and UX, and show the work that didn't fit in this post.

items.title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
items.summary:
This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib.  A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside [...]

Read More...

The post PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. 
  • A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems.
  • A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. 
  • For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed.

At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly.

In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding, data lineage, and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib, a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access.

PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows.

Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved.

PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. 

There are two kinds of modules: 

  • Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation.
  • Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. 

As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project.

Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale

PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta:

  • More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features.
  • Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library.
  • Millions of assets being accessed daily.
  • Billions of checks every second.

Operating at this scale creates three engineering challenges:

Challenge Approach
Coverage: Systems can have multiple client libraries and legacy integrations, accept direct network calls, and offer direct database access to backing stores. All of them need to be handled to ensure requirements hold no matter the access path. We integrate at two levels: typed client libraries, where PrivacyLib has full request context, and lower network boundaries on remaining RPC paths to get full coverage. Each integrated system maps its native APIs to PrivacyLib’s common operations and provides the inputs required by its configured modules. Once those pieces are in place, the same module can be enabled in multiple systems without a separate system-specific integration.
Scale: At billions of checks per second, even a small per-check computational cost becomes consequential across the fleet. Every service in the hot path pays that cost. We compile requirements at build time into their simplest evaluable form and answer most checks from caches inside the process, so the common path avoids a network call.
Reliability: Privacy logic runs in the hot path of critical systems, owned by teams that release on their own schedules. A change has to be testable in isolation and reversible on its own, because a fleet-wide rollback cannot be the recovery path. Enforcement is deployed as part of the service that owns it, so a change reaches production through that service’s own pipeline instead of a fleet-wide config push.


Walkthrough: Protecting Messaging Metadata

To illustrate how everything comes together at Meta’s scale, let’s walk through a privacy requirement that needs to be upheld when processing messaging metadata.

Users exchange messages through apps like Messenger, which supports end-to-end encryption. As Messenger routes and delivers those messages, subject to applicable law, its backend systems process non-content messaging data (i.e., messaging metadata), such as information about when messages are sent or delivered, to improve product performance, detect abuse, and protect users from harmful conduct. 

A variety of these backend services use Logger, a client library that runs in the service process, to write this metadata to data warehouse tables. Before writing a record, the PrivacyLib integration inside Logger invokes Policy Zones, an enforcing module, to check whether the metadata may flow to the destination table. This check is broken down into two parts: what inputs need to be available to make a decision, and how the check is actually evaluated at runtime. After examining these two parts, we look at how PrivacyLib scales across systems and how changes roll out without disrupting the services in the path.

Annotating Messaging Metadata

Every Logger destination table has a LoggerConfig that describes the records written to it. MetadataTraceLoggerConfig defines one such configuration for message-delivery traces and marks it as containing messaging metadata:

final class MetadataTraceLoggerConfig extends LoggerConfigBase {
  use MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait;
  public function configure(
    LoggerFieldDefiner $fd,
  ): LoggerFieldDefiner {
    $this->annotateWithTableLevelPolicy();
    // Field and destination definitions
  }
}

A logging destination can have many writers, so the annotation describing its output data belongs to the destination rather than to each service that writes to it. If every service declared the annotation separately, the declarations could disagree, or a new writer could omit it entirely. Declaring it once in LoggerConfig gives every writer the same description of the data.

For this destination, MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait supplies the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA table-level annotation, and annotateWithTableLevelPolicy() attaches it to the destination.

LoggerConfig is Logger’s own schema, and each system describes its data in its own format. To give PrivacyLib a single form to consume, Logger’s code-generation pipeline translates the configuration into a PrivacyLib-compatible artifact. The generated MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact is derived from MetadataTraceLoggerConfig and carries the destination identity and the messaging annotation:

/**
 * @codegen-source MetadataTraceLoggerConfig
 */
class MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact
  extends LoggerInputPrivacyLibArtifact {
  
  final public static function getAssetIDImpl(
  ): LoggerInputAssetID {
    return LoggerInputAssetID::get(
      'MetadataTraceLoggerConfig',
    );
  }

  protected static function getPurposePolicyVars(
  ): TPurposePolicyVars {
    return PurposePolicy::makeVars(
      TPurposePolicyName::MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA,
    );
  }

  // Other generated fields omitted.
}

The generated class above is used by Logger’s client in Hack, Meta’s typed PHP language. For its C++ and Python clients, Logger publishes destination identities and annotations to a central catalog. PrivacyLib uses that information to generate language-specific artifacts. In the C++ example in the next section, PrivacyLib uses the LoggerConfig name to load the C++ artifact for the destination.  

Running the Check

The artifact from the previous section describes one Logger destination. PrivacyLib also needs to know what a Logger write means and which modules should run. Logger’s Hack integration defines that once for all destinations:

$config->libraryConfig()->enablePrivacyLib(
  PrivacyLibOperation::write()
    ->input(
      PrivacyLibInput::instance(
        nameof ILoggerInputPrivacyLibPayloadProvider,
      ),
    )
    ->enforcements(
      PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::zones(
        ZoneDataType::LOGGER,
      )
        ->withPropagation()
        ->enabled(),
      PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::telemetryLogging()->enabled(),
      // Other modules
    ),
);

PrivacyLibOperation::write() declares PrivacyLib’s write operation for Logger, and enforcements() lists the modules that run on it. The Policy Zones module can affect the result, while the Telemetry Logging module records the evaluation without affecting it. Adding a module here requires no changes to individual destinations or Logger call sites. ZoneDataType::LOGGER tells Policy Zones that it is checking a Logger destination.

In C++ services, Logger constructs the PrivacyLib request as follows: 

const auto assetList =
      std::vector<std::string>{configName};

PrivacyLibBuilder builder(
      "LOGGER_WRITE_CLIENT",
      assetList,
      LoggerWriteAPIEnumHelper::apiToHashedString(
          PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log),
      Caller::LOGGER,
      getLoggerWriteImplementation());

auto result =
      PrivacyLibRequest(std::move(builder)).dispatch();

PrivacyLib uses configName to load the destination’s artifact. The hashed PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log value maps Logger’s API to PrivacyLib’s write operation. The remaining builder arguments identify Logger as the caller and provide the implementation that performs the write. dispatch() invokes the configured modules and records their outcomes. For the Policy Zones module, PrivacyLib provides the destination annotations from the generated artifact and the current processing context. For this example, Policy Zones evaluates two conditions:

  1. The current context represents an allowed use of messaging metadata.
  2. The destination artifact carries the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA annotation.

When enforcement is enabled, the Policy Zones module denies the write if either condition fails. PrivacyLib combines the results from enforcing modules into one response. A denial stops the write before Logger sends the record downstream. Observing modules emit telemetry without affecting the response.

Scaling Privacy Checks Across Systems

PrivacyLib enables privacy checks to scale across heterogeneous systems through a common execution model, lightweight evaluation and telemetry, and coverage for requests that bypass integrated clients. 

A Common Execution Model Across Systems

PrivacyLib’s integrations span systems with very different APIs: key-value stores, graph databases, ML pipelines, filesystems, and logging systems like Logger. Each integration maps its access points to one of five common operations, and PrivacyLib invokes its modules at each:

  1. Read: runs when fetching data.
  2. Write: runs when storing data.
  3. RPC: runs when calling another service.
  4. Request entry: runs once when a service begins handling a request.
  5. Inline execution: wraps a specific computation inside a larger request, such as evaluating a feature. Data accesses made during that computation are evaluated using its inline privacy context.

Modules are written against these five operations rather than against each system’s native API. Reads, writes, and RPCs also have post-operation variants, so observing modules can run after the access decision has been made. Once a system provides the mapping, every compatible module can reuse it, which is why enabling an additional module on an already-integrated system takes only days.

PrivacyLib runs inside the clients of data and processing systems because the clients already have the destination identity and request context that modules need. Keeping the evaluation in the same process avoids carrying those inputs across process boundaries on every access. This design also has two advantages:

  1. Richer context: PrivacyLib can use the caller’s identity, endpoint, and purpose while that information is still available. This information is frequently lost if the check is evaluated on the datastore.
  2. Failure isolation: A faulty change is contained to the service running that version of the code, keeping the shared datastore outside the failure boundary.

Keeping Checks Computationally Inexpensive

In-process evaluation must also be computationally efficient because it runs on every data access. Per-request caches eliminate repeated checks within a request and per-host caches retain frequently used configuration and results. This avoids the remote configuration fetch required by an earlier design (that fetch alone was thousands of times slower than the in-process path). The result is that PrivacyLib performs billions of checks per second across the fleet with low per-check latency, while consuming only a small fraction of Meta’s total compute capacity.

At PrivacyLib’s scale, telemetry must also remain lightweight. PrivacyLib records each module’s status, samples latency, and logs errors, giving us fleet-wide visibility into how enforcement is behaving in production. Recording every invocation in full detail would overwhelm the systems receiving those events, so the goal is to deduplicate repeated events while keeping rare ones visible. 

Two mechanisms work together to achieve this: Bloom filters on each host downsample high-volume patterns at a fixed rate, and fine-grained sampling rates adjust as traffic changes.

Covering Direct RPC Paths

Not every caller accesses data through a PrivacyLib-integrated client library; some issue raw RPCs. The RPC layer can still check those requests, but it sees far less context than the client does. PrivacyLib bridges that gap with a cryptographically-signed token: When a client-side check succeeds, PrivacyLib attaches the token to the request, and ServiceRouter validates it at a lower boundary for supported RPC traffic, confirming that the request already passed the richer client-side check.

When a request arrives at the RPC layer without a token, ServiceRouter falls back to a coarser check based only on the context visible in the network payload. Because that context is limited, the lower layer applies the strictest interpretation, choosing false positives over gaps. Between them, the two layers cover access through Meta-managed clients and supported RPC paths. Paths outside those boundaries are not covered by this mechanism and need their own PrivacyLib integration.

Together, the result is that evaluation stays local and computationally inexpensive wherever possible, with a coarser backstop where local evaluation is unavailable, and modules have one place to run across systems that otherwise share nothing. What remains is the harder operational question: how to change enforcement behavior without breaking live traffic or making incorrect access decisions.

Rolling Out Enforcement Changes Safely

Privacy requirements change over time. Updates to a destination’s annotation or an enforcing module can change whether a write is allowed. PrivacyLib has a safe rollout path for both types of changes.

Changing an Annotation

Adding or removing an annotation changes two lines in a LoggerConfig: the declaration that imports MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait and the call to annotateWithTableLevelPolicy(). Because the destination may have many writers, that two-line edit can begin blocking writes from many services at once.

Review is therefore built around showing the author and reviewers what the edit will actually do. During code review, Logger’s code-generation pipeline updates the destination’s PrivacyLib artifact. Simulations then replay observed data flows against both the new artifact and the existing one, and any flow whose result changes is reported. The source edit, the generated artifact, and the simulation results are reviewed together, so the decision rests on evidence of the change’s effect rather than only on reading the code change. If the simulation reports an unexpected change, reviewers hold the artifact before release.

Once approved, the artifact reaches services through their usual build and deployment pipeline. That gives two forms of visibility before the change is deployed, from the decision changes reported by the simulation and the generated code showing exactly what will be deployed, plus one form of control, since each service’s own deployment decides when the change reaches production. It also bounds the surface area: An issue found after deployment is limited to the services running that build.

The downside is that changes do not reach the entire fleet at once, making change propagation slower than a global configuration update. In practice, requirement owners use explicit tracking to update the services in scope by the required deadline, while a service that needs the update sooner can use its emergency deployment process.

Rolling Out a Module

An annotation change applies to one Logger destination. A module added to Logger’s write path runs for every Logger destination. We therefore deploy the module before enabling it across all traffic.

As an example, here is how Policy Zones was introduced on this path. We first set the Policy Zones module to rollingOut() in Logger’s PrivacyLib write-operation configuration:

PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::zones(ZoneDataType::LOGGER)
    ->rollingOut()

The rollout key, logger.input.write.zones, identified this combination of Logger input, write operation and the Policy Zones module. rollingOut() placed the module execution behind a runtime control. We then moved that control from 0 to 100% in stages while monitoring denials, errors, and latency. If valid writes began to fail, we could lower the percentage without rebuilding or redeploying the service. The Telemetry Logging module continues to run because it is configured independently. 

Once the Policy Zones module was stable across Logger traffic, we changed the configuration from rollingOut() to enabled(). At this point, the Logger integration ran the module without consulting the rollout percentage.

Safeguards apply at different stages across the two change paths described above. If a simulation shows unexpected flow changes, we hold the annotation artifact before release. If a module misbehaves after the rollout begins, we lower its rollout percentage using the runtime control.

These safety mechanisms changed what it takes to meet a privacy requirement at Meta. PrivacyLib now runs inside the clients of hundreds of data and processing systems and evaluates billions of checks every second, while consuming a small fraction of Meta’s compute. Requirements built on top of it, such as purpose limitation through Policy Zones and data flow discovery through Privacy Probes, reuse those integrations instead of rebuilding them, so enabling a module on systems that are already covered takes days rather than the months bespoke integrations used to take. When a change does go wrong, the failure stays inside the service running the deployed change. We can now use that foundation for a newer class of workload: AI agents.

PrivacyLib Controls for AI Agents

AI agents are harder to reason about than traditional services because their behavior is dynamic and the data they access is determined at runtime. Therefore, we have to design for agent safety up front by enforcing controls, such as Policy Zones, not only on what we expected the agents to access when we built them but also on what they attempt to access at runtime. Where enabled, these controls can block a disallowed access before any data is returned.

Agents invoke tools to carry out tasks. A single tool call may cross several services in a nested manner before reaching data. To tackle this new challenge, we built AgentLib, a common runtime based on PrivacyLib’s design principles, for observing and governing tool calls made by internal agents. On supported paths, AgentLib associates each tool call with its agent session, and downstream clients and services propagate that context until the call reaches a system integrated with PrivacyLib. At that data access boundary, PrivacyLib combines the context, the requested operation, and the destination’s annotations, then passes them to individual modules to make a final decision.

Within PrivacyLib, the Agent Observability module records the agent session and tool-call identifiers alongside the destination, client API, integration point, and any errors. Engineers can query these events by session to investigate the services and destinations involved in a tool call. When we introduced the Agent Observability module, PrivacyLib’s existing broad coverage enabled us to instrument systems already integrated with the library instead of manually integrating the module into hundreds of systems. Even with AI-assisted development, this would have been a daunting task. 

To enforce certain policies, we used the existing Policy Zones module without modification because it relies on the same inputs for enforcement. On paths where this control is enabled, it considers the destination annotations and agent context before allowing an operation. When Policy Zones blocks an operation, PrivacyLib propagates that result back through the call chain to the agent environment. Policy Zones applies this check even when the agent chooses a tool that its developer did not anticipate. The access decision does not depend on the agent behaving as intended.

Lessons Learned From Building and Operating PrivacyLib

Building and operating PrivacyLib across Meta’s systems taught us a few important lessons.

Design for evolving systems and requirements: Before PrivacyLib, we added privacy controls to the individual call sites needed to satisfy each new requirement. Over time, Meta built new data and processing systems, services gained new ways to process data, and privacy requirements expanded. Each change created more integration work, and new access paths sometimes appeared faster than we could cover them. The lesson was to integrate at a stable data access boundary, define the small set of operations that systems share, and keep annotations with the data. Modules can reuse the same integrations and reduce engineering effort over time.

Reliability earns adoption: Early on, an invalid config crashed processes across the fleet, breaking our own safe rollout principles. Other incidents came from annotation changes that compiled successfully but changed access decisions and caused product failures. These incidents showed that service owners will trust PrivacyLib in a critical data access path only when they can see how changes affect their traffic before release and recover from a problematic change without a fleet-wide rollback. 

Coverage includes deployment: When new requirements need changes to modules or supported policies and annotations, older services need to deploy versions with the updated PrivacyLib capabilities. We have ensured that explicit inventory, tracking, and rollout mechanisms are in place to coordinate these deployments, so that requirement owners can meet deadlines safely by updating only the services in scope.

Looking Forward

These lessons shape where we are taking PrivacyLib next, as AI pushes data access into environments and call paths that are increasingly novel. We continue to enrich PrivacyLib’s capabilities in two areas:

  1. AI training: Data used for training reaches our systems from a variety of environments. Much of it is produced or transformed in various places. We are extending PrivacyLib-style approaches to this domain so the same guarantees scale with it. For more on how Meta approaches AI training data, see AI at Meta: Transparency About Our Training Data.
  2. Internal AI agents: Observing attempted data accesses and blocking disallowed ones is just the starting point rather than a finished picture for agents used internally at Meta for engineering and productivity. The harder problems come next: evaluating internal agent behavior while it is happening, and reasoning about communication between these agents, where a single data access may be several agents removed from the person who asked for it.

Acknowledgements

The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of many current and former Meta employees who have played a crucial role in developing PrivacyLib over the years. In particular, we would like to extend special thanks to (in alphabetical order) Adwait Sathe, Andrew Vaslas, Darrien Glasser, Diana Marsala, Hanzhi Zhang, Kousik Nandy, Matthew Hillman, Matthieu Martin, Michael Dietz, Nathan Maue, Ramy Wassef, Sen Luo, Spencer Baumgardner, Vince Yang, and Zhong Hu. We would also like to express our gratitude to all reviewers of this post, including (in alphabetical order) Aleksandar Ilic, Alex Kagan, Alex Ponomarenko, Arash Nikkar, Avtar Brar, Chloe Lu, Chris Wiltz, Emil Vazquez, Emily Van Deuren, Rituraj Kirti, Sushaant Mujoo, and Wenlong Dong. We would like to especially thank Jonathan Bergeron for overseeing the effort and providing all of the guidance and valuable feedback, and Chloe Lu for pulling required support together to make this blog post happen.

items.title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
items.summary:
AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions

  • 01Science funders and societies
  • 02Institutions
  • 03Research projects and initiatives
  • 04What’s next

  • Published

    Oct 28, 2026

  • Category

    Announcements

We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

We’re sharing how this program has further scaled up from supporting individual scientists to developing a large number of scientific partnerships with institutions and foundations to support researchers across many scientific fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

Science funders and societies

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:

  • The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
  • The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
  • Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
  • Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
  • The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
  • CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS Registry®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Institutions

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

  • Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
  • Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
  • The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
  • Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
  • EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
  • Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

  • FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
  • LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
  • AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
  • gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
  • Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
  • Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

What’s next

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they [...]

Read More...

The post Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. 
  • Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. 
  • Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty.

For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next.

Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty.

Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey

This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities:

Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks.

Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them.

Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work, especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward.

AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs.

AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors

The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options.

Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else.

Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors:

“I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.”

“Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.”

When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help.

The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows.

Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity

Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does.

Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. Among 156 people who wrote their own answer, 22 described dynamic constructs, decorators, metaprogramming, or framework behavior. Ten described arrays, dataframes, or scientific typing, and at least eight described annotations that were inaccurate, incomplete, or too broad. Respondents repeatedly named Django, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, and Polars.

“Django does so much black magic it’s a wonder a type checker works at all.” — survey respondent

Library maintainers need annotations that capture how frameworks and data-science libraries behave. The Pyrefly team has been working with Quansight to improve third-party library typing, including contributions to pandas-stubs and NumPy.

Frequency of use changed which problems stood out. Among developers who used type hints rarely or sometimes, 41.6% found the type system too complex or verbose. The rate was 14.5% among developers who used type hints often or always. Missing library typing affected 36.2% of the lower-frequency group and 70.0% of the higher-frequency group.

“I use the straightforward parts and avoid the parts that are difficult to understand.” — survey respondent. 

Years of typing experience showed a different pattern. Complexity was reported by 18.2% of respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 16.0% with three to six years, and 21.0% with seven or more. Newer typing users were often regular users and experienced Python developers: Of the 396 respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 306 (77.3%) used type hints often or always and 345 (87.1%) had used Python for at least three years.

Guidance for developers who are new to typing should assume Python experience and show how to add types to an existing repository. Occasional users need a useful first check with little configuration and easy-to-understand errors. As we change the type system, we should aim to support more patterns without making common tasks harder.

Better Callable syntax is one practical place to start. It was the most selected missing feature, chosen by 45.7% of the 1,486 respondents who answered the question. The selection rate was similar for respondents who reported complexity and the rest of the sample.

Newer Checkers Gained Ground Quickly

Frequent type hint use remained between 85.5% and 88.0% across the three surveys: 88.0% in 2024, 85.9% in 2025, and 85.5% in 2026. A different group answered each year, but the overall rate remained consistent.

Checker choice was far less stable. When the 2024 Python Typing survey asked what feature was missing from the Python type system, one response now reads like a preview of the changes captured in this year’s results:

“A faster Mypy. Its lack of speed led to ecosystem fracturing and other type checkers don’t support Mypy plugins and behave differently in general.” – survey respondent

By 2026, developers had several newer open-source checkers to choose from. Speed or performance topped the reasons for choosing a checker, at 56.5%. Using the same list of checkers in both years, 49.9% selected two or more in 2026, up from 46.0% in 2025.

Developers Mix Checkers Across Their Workflows

Of the 700 respondents who selected Mypy, 297 also selected its editor plugin. Another 314 selected a different named checker integration without selecting the Mypy plugin.

Most Pyrefly respondents also selected another checker: 220 of 264, or 83.3%. In the free-text responses, developers described why their teams divide work between checkers:

“Because my team members use different IDEs, we use multiple type checkers for development, but rely on Mypy for linting (local and CI).” — survey respondent

“Locally we primarily use Pyright because it’s the only option we’ve tried that fully understands all the more niche typing patterns within our codebase. In CI/CD, we do a Pyrefly run and only run Pyright on files where Pyrefly fails, to improve performance of the check.” — survey respondent 

Among the 1,486 developers who answered the question about difficulties, 33.3% reported inconsistencies between checkers. Among the 738 respondents who selected multiple static checkers and answered the difficulty question, 315 (42.7%) reported inconsistencies between checkers.

IDE Support Remains Central as Typing Help Moves Away From Stack Overflow

Readability or documentation was the most selected reason to use type hints, chosen by 93.6% of 1,571 respondents. Editor support also ranked highly: 84.8% of the 1,494 people who gave it a numeric rating chose 4 or 5. About 39% of the 103 developers who supplied their own reason mentioned completion, navigation, hover information, or editor error messages.

“Drastically improves IDE tooltip/autocomplete.” – survey respondent 

Real-time editor feedback was widespread: 82.9% of 1,517 respondents ran a type checker in an editor. VS Code was the most selected editor or IDE, at 59.3%.

Where developers look for help has changed as well. From 2024 to 2026, Stack Overflow use fell from 46.4% to 22.9%, while large language model (LLM) chat rose from 26.0% to 41.7%. Python typing documentation rose from 56.2% to 65.9%. Checker-specific documentation ended at 60.5%, up from 52.2% after a dip in 2025. General Python documentation fell from 66.7% to 62.2%.

As developers move from Stack Overflow to typing- and checker-specific documentation, the quality of those sources matters more. Error messages should link to short, relevant explanations and examples. Links to documentation would also give LLM chat tools better information to work with.

Survey Results and Raw Data

Download the full results and data from the Python Typing Survey 2026.

Acknowledgements

The survey ran from August 5 through September 2, 2026. It was developed with support from the Pyrefly team at Meta, the PyCharm team at JetBrains, the Python team at Microsoft, the ty team at Astral/OpenAI, and community contributors on discuss.python.org. We shared it through Reddit, X, Mastodon, newsletters, the Python typing forum, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Discord, Slack, and type-checker project websites and social accounts. We lightly edited quotations for spelling, grammar, and punctuation. We thank everyone who responded, shared the survey, reviewed the data, or contributed to the Python typing community.
